I think AI and the fear of what AI can do—the anger at the AI data centers—I think things like that have really kind of taken over from the position that crypto occupied prior to Trump’s reelection in terms of the minds of the public. In terms of things that they’re really mad about. People remark, AI is a scam too. And I understand the mentality there, and I definitely think there are dynamics to that potential AI bubble that could be similar to the crypto bubble that popped. But AI is a fundamentally different technology that, you know, is having a real-world impact right now. Whereas crypto was the story of a technology that people didn’t understand, that didn’t work that well. Part of the problem is, even I have to—because I can’t do anything about it in the present, because I can’t hold Trump accountable in the present because of this dynamic with the DOJ—even I have to log off sometimes, just for mental health. I think if we’re gonna address the underlying issues with crypto—even just the crime—it’s gonna take years and years after Trump is out of office to sift through all of this stuff and hopefully hold people to account. But I do think it’s really important to hold people that have broken the law to account, whether they’re the president of the United States or not. Because if we don’t, then this trust that is our monetary system, that is our economic system, that is our government—that trust just breaks down. And we get kind of this environment where we feel like we can’t trust anything, you know. And people get really depressed and, to some, complacent, like, What can we do? Warzel: Which is a good environment for people to perpetuate grifts and scams and things like that, right? It is a cycle that perpetuates itself. If you get people into this situation where they feel powerless, without anything, and a complete distrust, then it’s easier to sell particular stories. One thing I wanted to address there with the AI stuff is: I agree with you that these things are not the same, in terms of AI is having this real-world impact. What I think is interesting, though, is the way that the griftier elements of crypto—of the web 3.0 and like Metaverse-style, you know, hype cycles—the way that those have actually impacted the way that a lot of people think about AI. Like, people are conditioned because they were sold this from the tech industry. Because the tech industry went all-in on the hype train on these things that had proven not really to have this value, or had proven to be scammy in certain ways. I think a lot of people are just conditioned to respond to this. And I think that the tech industry has also, very importantly, marketed a lot of artificial-intelligence stuff the same way that they tried to market a lot of the crypto stuff—which has led to people kind of associating them or feeling like the scam has to be there, even if it might not be. I wanted to ask though: What are some of the stories in crypto that you’re still tracking right now? Like, what are some of the loose ends? Because the way that I think of this conversation is: Your time, your investigation into this world, very much corresponds to the pandemic-era froth that sort of ends with the SBF stuff. And now we’re in this other realm, where crypto is kind of quiet in some ways but very influential. And so I’m just curious, like: What are some of the things that you’re still tracking? McKenzie: I’m really interested in this company Tether. It’s this massive stablecoin company that supposedly has something like 200 billion dollars of real money. Supposedly has more treasuries than Germany, the entire nation. It is a massive stablecoin company whose financial interests are represented by Cantor Fitzgerald, their broker. And Howard Lutnick, our commerce secretary, you know, was the head of Cantor. Now his sons run it. And Cantor owns a stake in Tether, as well as being its broker. Warzel: Explain to people what Tether is, real quick. McKenzie: It’s a stablecoin, meaning that it’s a cryptocurrency whose price is supposed to be stable. One Tether is always supposed to be worth one dollar. And they’re treated as sort of chips in the crypto casinos you can gamble on, but also these kind of synthetic dollars that can be sent anywhere in the world instantaneously. Criminals are able to use these stablecoins to get paid for their crimes, to coordinate with other criminals in other locations, and to avoid the banking system, because the stablecoins don’t have to run through a bank. There's a system in Southeast Asia called Hawala, where if you're trying to send money from a small village in India, you can send something of value by going to your local Hawala leader and they'll mark it down and then on the other end, the Hawala on the other will mark it down. It's a system of credit. And to me, stable coins are digital Hawala—it's a digital hawala system for international criminal cartels. And tethers are used for all sorts of, I mean, some of the worst criminal activity you can think of. They have just gotten bigger and bigger and bigger, you know. To the point where their interests are being advocated for in the White House by Lutnik, who raised an enormous amount of money for Trump so that he could be re-elected. I’m just interested in what happens with Tether. Warzel: How do you think about crypto right now? Is it losing steam compared to, you know, the boom times of 2021, 2022? Is it dormant? Is it hibernating? Has crypto shifted from something that regular retail investors were interested in to something that’s exclusively a vehicle for the currently rich? What is the state of it now? McKenzie: If you look at the Fed survey, the retail interest in terms of a percentage of the population peaked somewhere around 2021, 2022. It was never that high. I mean, I think in terms of legitimate pollsters that I’ve seen that have tried to pull this, it was maybe like 16 percent of the public had ever messed around with cryptocurrency. And most of those people are, you know, throwing in a few hundred bucks, like my buddy Dave. You know, hoping to get rich, but so they’re not really highly invested in it. But if you look at the Fed survey more recently, the number’s down. So the number of people in the general public that are buying this thing seems to be going down. And yet, crypto at the same time is working its way further into our regulated financial system and our political system through Trump—but in our economic system through these things called ETFs, exchange traded funds. Where a person, if they want to buy some bitcoin, they go to BlackRock. And BlackRock, which issues a bitcoin ETF, turns to a crypto exchange, Coinbase, and says, My client wants some bitcoin; hold it for us. The ETF market has gotten really big. And it’s also getting into our banking system, as you know. Trump has applied for a banking license. His family’s applied for a banking license. I think they’ve gotten a provisional license. The worry to me is not so much that there’s all these new converts out there, like, My God, I’m so excited. Who comes in now and is like, You know what I just heard about? Cryptocurrency. Like, you’d have to be pretty far off the—you know, Where have you been living, buddy? It’s more like—the virus is spreading into a different part of our body that’s even more delicate and could have far worse repercussions. I don’t know if that metaphor works, but the only thing that came to mind. Warzel: Yeah, the contagion is spreading; it’s scary. I think that’s a good place to leave it. Hopefully we can pick up on this conversation with whatever nightmares come next from crypto and our grand experiment with it. But Ben McKenzie: Thank you so much for coming on Galaxy Brain . It’s a delight. McKenzie: Yeah. Thanks for having me, Charlie. It was a good conversation. Warzel: That’s it for us here. Thank you again to my guest, Ben McKenzie. If you liked what you saw here, new episodes of Galaxy Brain drop every Friday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube channel or on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is that you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work and the work of my fellow journalists, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. That’s TheAtlantic.com/Listener. Thank you so much, and I’ll see you on the internet.

items.title: BoG to issue new Credit Risk Directive as NPL ratio in the Savings and Loans sector deteriorates
items.description: The Bank of Ghana (BoG) has announced plans to issue a Credit Risk Management Directive to strengthen lending practices, improve loan recovery and address rising non-performing loans (NPLs) in the financial sector. Second Deputy Governor Mrs Matilda Asante-Asiedu announced this on Wednesday, October 7, at the commissioning of Advans Ghana Savings and Loans’ new head office in Dzorwulu, Accra. She said the directive would require Regulated Financial Institutions (RFIs) to establish robust credit risk management frameworks covering credit underwriting, loan administration, risk measurement, monitoring, and recovery. “This directive aims to ensure that Regulated Financial Institutions (RFIs) develop and implement appropriate frameworks for managing their credit risk by establishing a robust credit risk environment; a sound credit-underwriting process; and maintaining appropriate credit administration, measurement, monitoring, and recovery processes and functions.” The directive will also set clear requirements for how institutions assess borrowers, manage credit risk and monitor loans, to reduce the accumulation of bad debts. Savings and loans NPLs rising against the industry trend. The announcement comes as the savings and loan sub-sector faces growing pressure to improve its loan portfolios. The BoG expects RFIs to bring their NPL ratios down to no more than 10% by the end of December 2026. Even as the industry-wide ratio improved, the sub-sector’s deteriorated. “The banking industry’s ratio stood at 16.1 per cent at end-June 2026, down from over 23 per cent a year earlier. However, for the Savings and Loans sub-sector, the NPL deteriorated from 15.35% in June 2025 to 19.44% for the same period in 2026. So, there is real work ahead of us in this last quarter to bring this in line with the regulatory expectation,” she said. The Deputy Governor noted that the BoG’s 2025 Notice on Non-Performing Loans had already set supervisory expectations for credit risk governance, prudential limits for NPL ratios and remedial measures for willful defaulters. The new directive reinforces these measures by requiring stronger credit risk management systems and more effective oversight of lending across the loan cycle. It complements existing regulatory measures to improve asset quality and strengthen the financial system. Broader reforms of the savings and loans and microfinance sub-sectors MMrsAsante-Asiedu said the directive is part of wider reforms to the savings and loans and microfinance sub-sectors. These sub-sectors, she said, have extended financial services to young people, women and micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), and have supported employment and financed businesses often overlooked by conventional banks. She stressed that a sector carrying that responsibility must be strong enough to bear it, which is why the BoG is reforming it. Under the reforms, the former Tier 1 to Tier 4 classification will be replaced by four categories, each with a defined mandate: Microfinance Banks Community Banks Credit Unions Last Mile Providers Existing savings and loans companies may transition into Microfinance Banks, which will be deposit-taking institutions serving MSMEs, groups and individuals. The reforms are to improve regulatory consistency, reduce opportunities for regulatory arbitrage and strengthen governance. Institutions in the same category will be held to the same standards, and boards and management teams will be required to demonstrate the necessary skills, expertise, and ethical standards. The Second Deputy Governor said the reforms should rebuild public confidence, deepen financial inclusion, attract investment, and strengthen local participation and ownership. created by photogrid December capital deadline Mrs Asante-Asiedu reminded existing institutions seeking to become Microfinance Banks that they have until December 31, 2026, to meet the minimum capital requirement of GH¢50 million. New entrants must meet GH¢100 million. Institutions may meet the requirement independently; merge with, or be acquired by, another institution; transfer their assets and liabilities to a qualified institution through an orderly process; or exit voluntarily. She commended Advans Ghana for its commitment to meeting the new capital requirements and praised the Advans Group for supporting its Ghanaian subsidiary. “We encourage other foreign shareholders to show a similar level of commitment to support their Ghanaian subsidiaries as all institutions work towards the end-of-year deadlines, for capital and for non-performing loans alike.” She called on financial institutions, government agencies, development partners, and customers to support the reform process, stressing that success depends on collective commitment to compliance, transparency, innovation, and professionalism. “The aim is a sector in which every institution is strong enough to protect its depositors and keep serving its clients.”

items.title: Rentrée scolaire 2026-2027 : des fournitures et du mobilier scolaire distribués par la tutelle
items.description: Le ministère de l’Éducation nationale a démarré l’opération de distribution de kits scolaires pour des élèves, selon un communiqué de la tutelle paru ce 9 octobre. Elle est conduite par la Direction de l’Administration générale et de l’Équipement (DAGE). Le ministère de l’Éducation Nationale a lancé une campagne de distribution de kits scolaires pour l’année scolaire 2026-2027. Le ministère a rendu public le communiqué ce 9 octobre. Ces kits sont composés de sacs à dos, de cahiers, de stylos, de crayons, de matériels de géométrie et d’ardoises. Les bénéficiaires de l’opération de dotation sont les élèves des Cours d’initiation (CI), ceux des classes de Sixième et de la Seconde. L’opération a été initiée par le ministre, Moustapha Guirassy et conduite par la direction de l’administration générale et de l’équipement. À travers cette distribution, « le ministère entend contribuer à alléger les charges liées aux fournitures scolaires qui pèsent sur les ménages mais également favoriser un démarrage effectif des enseignements-apprentissages dès le premier jour de la rentrée. » Le déploiement des kits a démarré le 11 septembre 2026 d’après le chef de la division de l’Administration générale et de l’Équipement (DAGE). Selon lui toujours, « toutes les circonscriptions de l’Éducation et de la Formation (IEF) vont recevoir leurs dotations. » Le communiqué a rappelé la dotation des lots importants de mobiliers scolaires qui avaient été envoyés dans les 14 académies pour équiper les CRFPE, les IME, les IA, les IEF, des lycées, des collèges, des écoles élémentaires et qui s’inscrit aussi dans la même dynamique. items.title: Met Office predicts rain, thunderstorms in upper, central regions from Oct 10-15
items.description: The Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) on Friday predicted rain, wind, and thunderstorms, along with isolated hailstorms, in the upper and central parts of the country from the weekend with occasional gaps. According to a press release issued by the PMD, a westerly wave is likely to enter upper parts of the country from Saturday and is likely to persist till Oct 15. Under the influence of the weather system, rain-windstorms and thunderstorms with isolated hailstorms are expected in the upper and central regions, including Kashmir, Gilgit-Baltistan (GB), Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab and the Islamabad region. According to the Met Office, these storms are expected at “isolated places” in Kashmir’s Neelum valley, Muzaffarabad, Rawalakot, Poonch, Hattian, Bagh, Haveli, Sudhanoti, Kotli, Bhimber and Mirpur, as well as GB’s Diamer, Astore, Ghizer, Skardu, Hunza, Gilgit, Ghanche and Shigar, from Oct 10-15 with occasional gaps. In KP, they are expected in Dir, Chitral, Swat, Kohistan, Shangla, Battagram, Mansehra, Abbottabad, Haripur, Buner, Malakand, Bajaur, Mohmand, Kohat, Peshawar, Charsadda, Nowshera, Mardan, Swabi, Khyber, Orakzai, Kurram, Hangu, Lakki Marwat, Karak, Bannu, Dera Ismail Khan and Waziristan for the same duration. The PMD forecast the same rain-windstorms, thunderstorms and isolated hailstorms in Islamabad, Rawalpindi, Murree, Galliyat, Attock, Chakwal, Jhelum, Mandi Bahauddin, Gujrat, Gujranwala, Hafizabad, Wazirabad, Lahore, Kasur, Sheikhupura, Sialkot, Narowal Mianwali, Khushab, Bhakkar, Sargodha, Jhang, Toba Tek Singh and Faisalabad from Oct 10-11 and 13-14, with occasional gaps. It added that they were also expected in Multan, Layyah, Dera Ghazi Khan, Bahawalpur, Bahawalnagar, Sahiwal, Okara, Pakpattan and Khanewal on Oct 10-11 and 13. The press release forecast “mainly hot and dry weather” in Balochistan, but predicted rain-wind and thunderstorms in isolated places in Zhob, Barkhan and Musakhel on Oct 10-11 and 13. “Mainly hot and dry weather is likely to continue” in Sindh in the coming days, the PMD added. The Met Office warned of the potential impacts of the weather system, noting that wind, hail and lightning could damage weak structures such as electric poles, solar panels, and the roofs or walls of kaccha houses during the forecast period. It also warned that hail might damage standing crops in the plains of Punjab and KP. The PMD also noted the possibility of light snowfall over high mountains and glaciers and added that daytime temperatures were likely to drop by 2-4 degrees Celsius during the forecast period. “Farmers are advised to manage their crop activities keeping in view the weather conditions,” it said. The Met Office further advised all concerned authorities to remain vigilant and take necessary measures to avoid any untoward situation during the forecast period. Earlier this week, heavy rains, strong winds and thunderstorms, with isolated hailstorms, were predicted in the upper parts of the country for Tuesday and Wednesday. A fresh spell of rain hit the country last month, particularly affecting Rawalpindi as inundated roads and knee-deep water at certain points exposed the city’s poor drainage system. Islamabad and Rawalpindi received another burst of heavy rain at the end of September, with civic departments in the garrison city placed on high alert. Earlier that month, KP also witnessed rain as heavy downpours lashed Mohmand, damaging and flooding roads and creating difficulties for residents. Rain coupled with strong winds and dust had also damaged vegetable and maize crops in Bajaur district, but no casualties were reported.

items.title: 2023 election loss led me to become pastor — Banky W
items.description: Nigerian singer, filmmaker and politician Bankole Wellington, popularly known as Banky W, has said his defeat in the 2023 House of Representatives election left him heartbroken and prompted him to seek a new direction, eventually leading him into pastoral ministry. Banky W disclosed this while reflecting on his first anniversary as a pastor in the United States, where he said the electoral setback forced him to surrender his plans to God and reconsider his purpose. “In 2023 I lost an election. And while the experience inspired me in many ways, it also broke my heart into a million little pieces,” he wrote on Instagram. The entertainer said he turned to God after the election to seek direction and surrender his ambitions. “When the dust settled, I took those pieces back to God. And I surrendered,” he said. According to him, the experience made him question whether he should focus on leadership, entertainment, business or ministry. However, he said he eventually realised that he did not have to choose one path at the expense of the others. “And somewhere along the way, I realised that I was asking God to choose between things He had never asked me to separate,” Banky W said. “It wasn’t either/or. It was all of the above.” He added that his transition into pastoral ministry had changed his understanding of purpose, saying he now saw his responsibilities as expanding rather than narrowing. “Turns out, God wasn’t trying to put me in a box. He was expanding my assignment,” he said. Banky W explained that he now combines his responsibilities as a pastor and professor with his work as a filmmaker, musician and entrepreneur. He also recalled joking about his possible future in ministry, saying he had previously insisted that the letter “P” in his name, P. Banks, stood for professor rather than pastor. “I used to joke that the ‘P’ in P. Banks stood for Professor, not Pastor. I guess God heard and said, ‘Why not both?’” he wrote. The singer also spoke about the challenges of travelling regularly between Lagos and the Washington, DC, Maryland and Virginia area to manage his various responsibilities. “Constantly travelling back and forth between Lagos and the DMV isn’t always easy. But has it been worth it? Absolutely,” he said. Reflecting on the past year, Banky W said the experience had taught him that setbacks could lead to unexpected opportunities. “One year later, I’m reminded that sometimes what feels like the end of your story is really just God turning the page,” he said. “The election didn’t go the way I hoped. But God’s plans for my life are bigger than the plans I had for myself.” Banky W contested the 2023 House of Representatives election to represent Eti-Osa Federal Constituency in Lagos State on the platform of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP). He lost to Thaddeus Attah of the Labour Party. The post 2023 election loss led me to become pastor — Banky W appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: You can preach in a stationary vehicle, but not when it’s moving – Mahama clarifies
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has clarified that the government has not banned preaching in vehicles, insisting that the Road Traffic Regulations, 2026 (L.I. 2519), are intended to protect the safety of drivers and passengers. Speaking for the first time on the controversy surrounding Regulation 141 of the Legislative Instrument, he said preaching and selling were prohibited only in moving vehicles and could take place when vehicles were stationary. “The driver’s mind may be focused on what you are preaching, and you could fall if the driver suddenly applies the brakes.” – President John Mahama explains why preaching in public or commercial vehicles must stop once the vehicle begins moving. #JoyNews https://t.co/n5krHcB8cJ — JoyNews (@JoyNewsOnTV) October 9, 2026 “It has come to my attention that there is a perception that we have banned preaching in vehicles. What we are saying is that no one should preach or sell in a moving vehicle. Regardless of your faith, you cannot preach in a moving vehicle, but you can preach when the vehicle is stationary. It is not true that we have banned preaching in vehicles,” he stated. Regulation 141 prohibits preaching and hawking in public and commercial vehicles while they are in motion. Offenders face fines ranging from 10 to 50 penalty units, imprisonment for up to eight months, or both. The provision has attracted criticism from some religious leaders and members of the public, who have raised concerns about its implications for evangelism and religious expression. President Mahama said the restriction was intended to prevent activities that could distract drivers and expose passengers, preachers and traders to danger. Meanwhile, the government has suspended the implementation of the provision following the public backlash and is holding further consultations on the regulation.

items.title: Meet Ekiti driver Adeleke Adeniyi who borrowed N3.5m to campaign for Tinubu
items.description: By Enitan Abdultawab Adeleke Adeniyi, a mini truck driver in Ado Ekiti, the Ekiti State capital, has said he borrowed N3.5 million to support the re-election campaigns of President Bola Tinubu, Senate Leader Opeyemi Bamidele and a member of the Ekiti State House of Assembly, Steve Fatoba. Adeniyi disclosed this in a video shared by Ekiti State Television (EKTV) on Facebook, where he displayed a Wema Bank cheque showing N2 million for Tinubu, N1 million for Bamidele and N500,000 for Fatoba. Explaining his decision, the driver said he was convinced that Tinubu deserved another term because of his administration’s performance. “I am supporting Mr President, Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu, for his second-term ambition. I have borrowed money. I want to use this money to support him because he’s doing a very great job,” he said. Adeniyi also pledged to campaign for the president and said he intended to use a song to promote Tinubu’s re-election bid. “I am fully ready to go out to campaign for him. And I’m going to use this song to back him up. On your mandate, we shall stand,” he added. Appealing to Nigerians to vote for Tinubu in the next presidential election, Adeniyi expressed optimism that a second term would bring further benefits to the country. “I will appeal to my fellow Nigerians that we should demonstrate love by giving him, by voting him for his second term in office, because we are still going to see much more, more than what we have received,” he said. The driver also praised Bamidele, saying the senator’s support for projects in Ekiti had encouraged him to back his political ambitions. Describing the federal lawmaker as a good leader, Adeniyi said the projects he had supported made a positive impression on him. “Most times, I look at the kind of projects that you always put on; you always supported. It always encouraged me that, no, indeed, this is a good leader,” he said. Adeniyi operates around the BAO Timber Market along Ilawe Road in Ado Ekiti. The latest move follows a similar show of support in February, when he reportedly borrowed money through the digital lending platform OPay to brand a vehicle in support of the second-term ambition of Biodun Oyebanji, governor of Ekiti State. The post Meet Ekiti driver Adeleke Adeniyi who borrowed N3.5m to campaign for Tinubu appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: L’homosexualité dans le monde en 2026 : un état des lieux
items.description: En 2026, 29,2 % de la population mondiale vit toujours sous un régime qui criminalise, à des degrés divers, les relations sexuelles entre personnes de même sexe. Dans le même temps, plus de la moitié de l’humanité vit dans des États qui ne disposent ni de cadre légal relatif à l’union des personnes homosexuelles ni ne criminalisent les relations entre celles-ci. Il y a là le résultat de deux tendances croisées depuis le tournant des années 1990. D’une part, un nombre croissant de pays adoptent des dispositifs d’union civile et/ou de mariage pour les personnes de même sexe. D’autre part, les États qui criminalisent ces relations ont vu leur nombre diminuer de 114 en 1990 à 65 en 2025. De ce point de vue, les dispositifs coloniaux continuent de laisser leur marque : la plupart des pays qui criminalisent encore les relations sexuelles entre personnes de même sexe le font sur le fondement de dispositions juridiques héritées de la colonisation, qui soit ont été conservées telles quelles, soit ont servi de fondement à l’extension du cadre juridique criminalisant l’homosexualité. Les progrès constatés ne vont toutefois pas sans entraves. Si la contraction de la criminalisation souligne des progrès indéniables, elle ne doit pas cacher le renforcement ces dernières années, dans certains États, comme c’est le cas au Sénégal, au Mali, au Burkina Faso ou au Niger, de législations à l’encontre des personnes homosexuelles. Par ailleurs, certains États, à l’instar de la Russie, qui ne criminalisent pas ou plus l’homosexualité, peuvent être le théâtre d’obstacles juridiques à la liberté d’association autour des questions de diversité sexuelle, de genre et corporelle. En 2026, les personnes homosexuelles risquent encore la peine de mort dans onze pays. ILGA World, fédération d’associations de défense des droits des personnes LGBTI+, disposant d’un statut consultatif auprès du Conseil économique et social des Nations unies ne retient pas une certitude juridique complète quant à l’applicabilité de la peine de mort dans cinq États – Afghanistan, Pakistan, Qatar, Somalie et Émirats arabes unis –, en raison de l’absence de fondement juridique explicite et de divergences doctrinales relatives à l’interprétation de certaines dispositions. Cette incertitude concerne exclusivement le niveau de la sanction encourue : la criminalisation y est bien juridiquement établie. Un état des lieux, en carte et infographie, des cadres légaux qui régissent les relations entre personnes de même sexe à travers le monde. L’article L’homosexualité dans le monde en 2026 : un état des lieux est apparu en premier sur IRIS .

items.title: Bamako : un assassinat présumé relance le débat sur les violences faites aux femmes
items.description: Le deces d'une jeune femme retrouvee morte par balle a son domicile conjugal a Bamako, suscite une vive emotion. L'Association pour le progres et la defense des droits des femmes (APDF) condamne le drame et appelle les autorites a appliquer rigoureusement les sanctions prevues contre les violences faites aux femmes. L'affaire suscite de nombreuses reactions sur les reseaux sociaux. La presidente nationale de l'APDF, Diawara Bintou Coulibaly, condamne les faits et demande que justice soit rendue . « L'acte, quand meme, a ete commis et nous le condamnons. Nous souhaitons que la personne soit condamnee, parce que ce sont des exemples que nous ne devons pas encourager » , declare-t-elle. « Des sanctions existent, mais leur application pose probleme » Pour Diawara Bintou Coulibaly, la lutte contre les violences faites aux femmes necessite, au-dela des campagnes de sensibilisation, une application effective des sanctions. « Il y a des sanctions, mais c'est leur application qui pose probleme. Nous demandons aux autorites d'appliquer les sanctions necessaires pour qu'on puisse arreter ces violences » , insiste-t-elle. La presidente de l'APDF affirme que plusieurs femmes ont ete tuees au Mali. Selon les informations dont dispose son association, huit a neuf femmes auraient ete victimes de ces violences. Presomption d'innocence : le rappel d'un juriste L'interpellation du mari de la victime a egalement suscite de nombreuses reactions. Toutefois, le juriste Ibrahim Khalid Toure rappelle que toute personne soupconnee d'un crime beneficie de la presomption d'innocence jusqu'a ce que sa culpabilite soit etablie par la justice. « Une personne accusee ou suspectee peut jouir de la presomption d'innocence tant qu'il n'y a pas de condamnation definitive » , explique-t-il. Il precise que la decouverte eventuelle d'une arme sur les lieux ou la mise en detention d'un suspect ne suffit pas, a elle seule, a etablir sa culpabilite. Le juriste souligne ainsi que le mandat de depot ne constitue pas une declaration de culpabilite. Il appartient a la justice d'examiner les elements de l'enquete et de determiner les responsabilites. Le deces de cette jeune dame ravive les preoccupations autour des violences conjugales et des violences mortelles faites aux femmes au Mali. items.title: Alhaji Iddrisu Mustapha: The educated professional seeking to bring experience to NDC Western Region leadership
items.description: Alhaji Iddrisu Mustapha (AIM), an aspirant for the position of Western Regional Vice Chairman of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), is seeking to draw on his background in education, energy policy and corporate affairs in his bid for the party position. His academic and professional background spans teacher training, university education, postgraduate studies in the United Kingdom and participation in international programmes on energy, climate change and development. Academic background Alhaji Mustapha began his education at Nuriya English and Arabic Basic School before attending Business Senior Secondary School (BISCO) in Tamale, where he obtained his Senior Secondary School Certificate between 1993 and 1995. He subsequently trained as a professional teacher at E.P. Training College, completing his programme in 1999. In 2007, he obtained a Bachelor of Education in Social Sciences from the University of Cape Coast (UCC), graduating with Second Class Upper Division. He majored in Management and minored in Accounting. He later pursued a Master of Science in Energy Management, specialising in the oil and gas route, at Robert Gordon University in Aberdeen, United Kingdom, graduating with merit in 2012. His master’s research examined ways to promote solar cooling technology in commercial and residential buildings in Ghana, with the aim of reducing reliance on the national electricity grid for cooling. He also participated in the International Summer School at the University of Oslo in Norway in 2018, obtaining a certificate in Energy, Environment and Social Change. In 2021, he completed a Climate Reality Leadership Corps training programme and became a Climate Reality Advocate under the initiative founded by former United States Vice President Al Gore. His professional development has also included an International Executive Development Programme in Communication Skills and Promotion of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, organised by the National Institute for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises in Hyderabad, India. Professional experience Alhaji Mustapha currently serves as Principal Corporate Affairs Officer at the Minerals Development Fund (MDF), a position he assumed in May 2026. Before joining the fund, he worked as an Energy Policy Analyst at the Energy Policy and Research Institute, a civil society organisation, from 2015 to 2022. From 2007 to 2012, he served as Deputy Regional Manager of Schools at the Islamic Education Unit of the Ghana Education Service. His work across these institutions has involved education administration, energy policy and corporate affairs. International programmes and conferences Alhaji Mustapha has participated in several international conferences and professional programmes. In 2025, he attended the Global Conference on Biodiversity Conservation and Climate Mitigation in Santa Clara, California, in the United States. He also participated in the Energy: Ensuring Africa Electrifies in a World of Shocks programme organised by Unstoppable Africa, the Global Africa Business Initiative, as a side event of the 80th United Nations General Assembly in New York. He was also involved as a coordinator and organiser of a high-level side event during the General Assembly on Unlocking Africa’s Financial Sovereignty: Strengthening African Financial Architecture in a New Global Order . Additionally, he participated in the 9th NYC Green School Conference, which focused on pupils, the planet, progress, partnerships and prosperity. Plans for further studies Alhaji Mustapha has also secured admission to pursue a PhD in Energy and Power at Cranfield University in the United Kingdom. However, the programme has been put on hold because of financial constraints, according to his profile. Bid for NDC regional leadership Alhaji Mustapha’s bid for the Western Regional Vice Chairman position comes as the NDC prepares for its internal electoral process in the region. His campaign highlights his education and professional experience as part of the background he would bring to the party’s regional leadership. His experience in education administration, energy policy and corporate affairs covers areas relevant to public administration, stakeholder engagement and economic development. His campaign uses the slogans “People Servant”, “AIM4Power” and “The Obvious Choice” to communicate his message to party delegates. The contest will determine who assumes the position of Western Regional Vice Chairman and takes on the responsibilities associated with the party’s regional administration and organisation.

items.title: Drone strikes and deadly explosions kill scores of civilians across Sudan
items.description: Drone strikes and explosions have killed scores of civilians and injured dozens across Sudan, as attacks on displacement shelters and residential neighbourhoods in Blue Nile and North Kordofan coincide with deadly mine blasts in West Kordofan and renewed armed violence in South Darfur. In Blue Nile, the regional government reported that 30 civilians were killed on Friday morning when the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) launched a drone attack on a displacement shelter in Abu Shandi, a village in Wad El Mahi locality. However, the Emergency Lawyers group reported preliminary information indicating that eight children had been killed and 26 women seriously injured, with the full toll remaining unclear. Residents told Radio Dabanga that most of the victims were women and children. The shelter housed people who had fled Geisan locality in search of safety. The Blue Nile Regional Government held the RSF responsible for the attack and urged the international community, human rights organisations and humanitarian agencies to condemn the killings, investigate the incident and hold those responsible accountable. The Emergency Lawyers group also condemned the strike, describing it as a serious escalation in attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure . It called for an immediate halt to such attacks and an independent, transparent investigation. Displaced people arrive in Geisan locality, Blue Nile – March 2026 (File photo: Blue Nile Emergency Room) ‘Displacement mounts’ The attack comes amid worsening insecurity across Blue Nile. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) reported that a further 1,275 people, or 255 families, had fled 10 villages in Wad El Mahi locality as the security situation deteriorated. The displaced moved to different locations in El Roseires locality. In Ed Damazin, residents reported further displacement following drone strikes and ground attacks in several areas. One resident told Radio Dabanga that the regional government was urging people to remain in the city despite the insecurity. The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) Fourth Infantry Division and allied forces said they had repelled an attack by the RSF and the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North in the Umm Darfa area of eastern Blue Nile. ‘Drone strike injures six in El Obeid’ In North Kordofan, an RSF drone attack on El Obeid on Friday morning injured six civilians, who were taken for treatment. The strike also damaged residential houses and destroyed six vehicles, according to the report. The latest attack follows a separate strike on a shelter for internally displaced people in El Obeid last week, in which five people were killed. The SAF and the RSF have continued to exchange drone attacks, killing civilians and damaging essential infrastructure. Unexploded ordnance (UXO) found in West Darfur’s capital of El Geneina in June, 2023 (File photo: RD) ‘UXO blast kills four in Babanusa’ In West Kordofan, four displaced people were killed earlier this week when an unexploded landmine detonated in Babanusa, bringing the reported mine-related death toll in the city to about 35. More than 20 people, including children and adults, have reportedly suffered amputations, while around 70 cattle have also been killed in mine explosions. Howaida Abdelrahman Saleh, executive director of the Muznah charitable organisation, told Radio Dabanga that the four victims had travelled to Babanusa to settle there after hearing that relief aid had arrived. They went to the military division’s headquarters to collect supplies for their family when a mine exploded, killing them immediately. Saleh warned that mines and explosive remnants of war scattered throughout houses and residential neighbourhoods, particularly around the division’s headquarters, had turned Babanusa into a “time bomb”. She said the widespread contamination posed a serious threat to returning residents and newly displaced people, some of whom enter dangerous areas in search of beds and other household essentials. Continued population movements have made efforts to manage the risks increasingly difficult. Muznah carried out mine-risk awareness activities in four Babanusa neighbourhoods in early September: El Salam, El Wahda, Maqat El Sharq and Maqal El Gharb. The initiative reached more than 300 school students and included awareness sessions in markets, mosques and livestock markets, as well as warning signs near high-risk areas. Saleh urged residents not to touch suspicious objects and to report them immediately to the police so that specialist teams could respond. She also called for urgent mine clearance , stronger public awareness campaigns and additional support for Babanusa Hospital, which has resumed operations but lacks the resources to meet residents’ needs. Darfur gunman (File Photo: Albert González Farran / UNAMID) ‘Armed clashes kill 11 in South Darfur’ In a separate incident in South Darfur , 11 people were killed in armed clashes in Wad El Fursan on Thursday evening following a dispute between an RSF force and a motorcycle trader. A local source told Radio Dabanga that the dispute began when a man who had reported the theft of his motorcycle to the police identified a suspect in the market. An RSF officer, El Nazir Hilal, accompanied by two guards, went with the man to confront the suspect, who said he had bought the motorcycle from a local dealer. The force then approached the dealer and asked him to accompany them to the police station. When the dealer requested time to complete the delivery of motorcycles in his showroom to their owners, the force refused. A further dispute erupted after the dealer offered to leave a relative in custody until he had finished the deliveries. According to the source, the dealer shot and killed the officer and one other member of the force, while another member of the force shot and killed the dealer. Subsequent clashes during the night brought the death toll to 11. The fighting heightened fears of further violence, although the source said the security situation had stabilised by Friday morning following the arrival of reinforcements from Nyala, the state capital. items.title: Roi Mohammed VI : le modèle actuel de coopération migratoire est dépassé
items.description: Le Roi Mohammed VI a évoqué les relations entre le Maroc et l'Espagne notamment dans le dossier de l'immigration, dans son discours en ouverture de la première session de la 12ème législature. Le souverain a affirmé que le Maroc joue un rôle important dans la gestion de l’immigration, mais que les accords actuels ne sont plus adaptés aux réalités d’aujourd’hui. Dans son discours devant les nouveaux députés élus à la suite des législatives du 23 septembre, le Roi Mohammed VI a déclaré que « l'approche équilibrée adoptée par notre pays dans la gestion de la question migratoire a donné des résultats positifs et fructueux ». Toutefois, a-t-il estimé, cette coopération avec l'Espagne fait aujourd’hui face à des défis majeurs, liés à certaines dispositions juridiques obsolètes et à des décisions judiciaires éloignées de la réalité. « Nous devons reconnaître avec courage et objectivité que le modèle actuel de coopération dans ce domaine est devenu dépassé », a affirmé le souverain en soulignant que les accords en vigueur en témoignent clairement. Ainsi, le Roi a annoncé que le Maroc proposera à ses partenaires un document présentant une vision stratégique claire et pragmatique, destinée à établir une nouvelle approche fondée sur le renforcement du développement partagé, de la compétitivité économique et de la stabilité régionale. items.title: Le Roi adresse un discours au Parlement à l'occasion de l'ouverture de la 1ère session de la première année législative de la 12e Législature
items.description: Le Roi Mohammed VI, que Dieu L'assiste, accompagné de SAR le Prince Héritier Moulay El Hassan, de SAR le Prince Moulay Rachid et de SA le Prince Moulay Ahmed, a adressé, vendredi, un discours au Parlement à l'occasion de l’ouverture de la première session de la première année législative de la 12e Législature. Voici le texte intégral du Discours Royal : « Louange à Dieu, Paix et Salut sur le Prophète, Sa Famille et Ses Compagnons. Mesdames, Messieurs les honorables parlementaires, L’ouverture de la nouvelle législature est l’occasion pour Nous de féliciter les membres de la Chambre des Représentants pour la confiance que leur ont témoignée les électeurs. Cette mandature intervient dans une conjoncture exceptionnelle, riche en opportunités qui pourraient ne pas se renouveler et qu’il convient de saisir pour poursuivre la dynamique de réalisations dans les différents domaines. S’agissant du nouveau mandat législatif et gouvernemental, Nous attendons qu’il constitue un véritable tournant pour un Maroc soucieux de poursuivre son ambition de puissance économique émergente et fiable et tout aussi attaché à trouver un équilibre harmonieux entre les logiques de croissance économique et les impératifs d’une justice sociale et spatiale renforcée. Mesdames, Messieurs, En 2014, à cette même tribune, J’avais déclaré que : « le sentiment qui M'est le plus cher dans la vie, c'est celui d'être fier de Ma marocanité » […] Aujourd’hui encore, le même sentiment demeure intact, et les années passant, il ne fait que croître et s’enraciner davantage. De fait, le Maroc, l’une des nations les plus prestigieuses et les plus anciennement constituées du monde, prospère sous la houlette de l’une des plus anciennes monarchies de l’histoire. Sous l’égide de la Commanderie des Croyants, les Marocains ont tout à fait raison de se sentir fiers de l’authenticité de notre identité religieuse, ainsi que de la singulière richesse de leur civilisation aux affluents divers et multiples. Nous avons aussi de quoi être fiers, au vu de nos acquis politiques et diplomatiques, des progrès économiques et sociaux et des niveaux de développement qui ont changé la physionomie du Maroc. La fierté nationale, ici, n’est pas une forme de vanité, ni l’expression d’une autosatisfaction. Elle est plutôt le catalyseur qui transforme l’appartenance en responsabilité, l’assurance en devoir national. Mesdames, Messieurs, Dans un contexte international marqué par l’accélération des mutations géoéconomiques, Notre pays s'est engagé, avec une vision claire, dans une nouvelle dynamique de réformes et de grands chantiers. Aujourd’hui, outre l’activation des projets d’infrastructures à l'ordre du jour, une nouvelle génération de grandes stratégies doit être lancée, notamment dans les secteurs de la sécurité hydrique, énergétique et alimentaire, de l’émergence industrielle, de l’économie numérique et de l’intelligence artificielle. Par ailleurs, Nous appelons de nouveau à une plus grande célérité dans le développement des capacités du Royaume en matière de constitution des réserves stratégiques et de sécurisation de l’approvisionnement en produits de première nécessité. A cet égard, Nous exhortons le secteur privé à renforcer son rôle en tant qu’acteur stratégique de la transformation qui s’opère dans notre pays à la faveur de son développement. Nous l’engageons aussi à se montrer plus entreprenant, plus créatif et plus apte à créer des opportunités d’emploi et à développer ses capacités d’investissement et d’exportation. Il convient également de placer les questions liées à la jeunesse en tête des politiques publiques et des préoccupations des instances de gouvernance, à travers l’élaboration d’une vision intégrée garantissant l’égalité des chances et couvrant l’éducation, la qualification et l’insertion économique. Les jeunes seront ainsi plus assurés de leur capacité à monter dans l’échelle sociale et auront davantage foi dans les institutions de leur pays et dans les opportunités qui leur sont offertes pour bâtir un avenir meilleur dans un cadre garant de liberté, de dignité et de stabilité. Mesdames, Messieurs, L'enjeu réel de la prochaine étape est l’action territoriale qui devra être menée sur le terrain pour identifier les vrais problèmes de chaque région et pour leur trouver des solutions réalistes. En effet, la promotion du développement intégré, l’amélioration de la qualité des services publics et l’encouragement de l’investissement productif sont étroitement liés au processus de régionalisation avancée et à la mise en œuvre de la déconcentration administrative. Or le retard et les dysfonctionnements qui freinent toujours l’opérationnalisation de la décentralisation et de la déconcentration affectent les programmes de développement socio-économique et empêchent de répondre aux préoccupations réelles des citoyens. Aussi, Nous soulignons avec force qu'aucun retard ni atermoiement n'est plus tolérable dans la mise en œuvre pleine et entière de la Charte de la Déconcentration, avec ce que cela implique en termes de transfert des compétences et de réaffectation des ressources humaines et financières nécessaires du Centre vers les provinces et les régions. De même, il convient de lever les obstacles qui continuent d’entraver le fonctionnement des institutions de la Région, notamment en définissant plus clairement les compétences y afférentes et en renforçant leurs effectifs humains et leurs ressources matérielles. En effet, il devient indispensable de mieux organiser les relations entre l'Etat et les régions et d'instaurer les mécanismes de coordination et de contractualisation nécessaires pour doter celles-ci du pouvoir de décision et d’exécution des projets. Mesdames, Messieurs, Le Royaume a pu conforter sa position à l’international, en tant que partenaire responsable, fiable, soucieux d'honorer ses engagements et parfaitement fondé, par voie de conséquence, à recevoir le même traitement de la part de ses partenaires. En outre, l'approche équilibrée que notre pays a adoptée dans la gestion du phénomène migratoire a abouti à des résultats concrets. Cependant, nous devons reconnaître, avec courage et objectivité qu’en la matière, le modèle actuel de coopération a atteint ses limites, comme en attestent clairement les crises récurrentes. La même analyse est valable pour notre voisine, l’Espagne, avec laquelle notre partenariat a connu d’importantes avancées dans les différents domaines, y compris dans la lutte contre l’immigration irrégulière. Néanmoins, cette coopération se heurte aujourd’hui à des défis majeurs, liés à certaines dispositions légales dépassées et à des décisions judiciaires éloignées de la réalité. Malheureusement, un tel attelage entrave le rapatriement des mineurs et des personnes usurpant le statut de réfugié, et aiguise l’appétit des réseaux criminels. Face aux déclarations irresponsables de certains milieux politiques et médiatiques et à leur instrumentalisation flagrante de la situation, Nous affirmons que le partenariat est un choix souverain et un engagement volontaire, qui ne saurait faire l’objet d’aucune pression ou menace, ni d’aucun chantage. Dans ce cadre, le Maroc présentera à ses partenaires un document dans lequel sera exposée une vision stratégique, claire et pratique, porteuse d’une orientation nouvelle visant à promouvoir le co-développement, la compétitivité économique et la stabilité régionale. Mesdames, Messieurs les parlementaires, Ainsi que vous le savez, le mandat parlementaire est un engagement politique et un contrat moral qui vous lie aux citoyens. Soyez donc, que Dieu vous garde, à la hauteur de cette responsabilité nationale dont vous répondez devant Dieu, les citoyens et l’histoire, et dont vous serez rétribués comme promis dans la parole du Très-Haut : « Quiconque viendra avec une bonne action aura dix fois son équivalent ». Véridique est la parole de Dieu. Wassalamou alaikoum warahmatoullahi wabarakatouh ». items.title: CAF considering return to biennial AFCON – Motsepe
items.description: The Confederation of African Football (CAF) is considering a return to the traditional two-year cycle for the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON), less than a year after announcing plans to hold the continent’s flagship football tournament every four years. CAF President Patrice Motsepe confirmed the development on Friday during a press conference in Cape Verde, on the final day of the organisation’s Strategy Conference. “‘We are looking at everything, including bringing the AFCON back to every two years,” Motsepe said. In December 2025, CAF announced that AFCON would move from its traditional biennial schedule to a four-year cycle after the 2028 edition. Under the plan, the 2027 tournament, scheduled to be co-hosted by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda, would proceed as planned, followed by another edition in 2028 before the new format took effect. As part of the restructuring, CAF also announced plans to introduce an African Nations League in 2029. The governing body said the new competition would ensure that Africa had a major senior men’s national-team tournament every year outside FIFA World Cup years. However, the decision to move AFCON to a four-year cycle attracted criticism from across the continent. Motsepe defended the change in January, rejecting claims that FIFA had pressured CAF to alter the tournament’s frequency. His latest comments indicate a possible shift in the organisation’s position, although he stopped short of announcing a formal reversal. A return to the two-year format could require CAF to reconsider aspects of its competition calendar, including plans for future editions of AFCON and the proposed African Nations League. CAF has already opened the bidding process for the 2028, 2032 and 2036 editions of AFCON. However, the organisation has yet to explain how a possible return to the biennial schedule would affect those plans or when a final decision would be announced. The discussions took place during CAF’s three-day Strategy Conference in Cape Verde, which brought together presidents of all 54 member associations, Executive Committee members, national-team coaches and other football officials. The conference focused on the continent’s football priorities and strategic direction through 2030. Lutte contre la dengue au Burkina Faso : Des professionnels des médias formés pour renforcer la prévention
items.description: Face à la persistance de la dengue au Burkina Faso, l’information apparaît comme un autre front de la prévention. C’est dans cette perspective qu’une trentaine de professionnels des médias ont été formés, du 5 au 7 octobre 2026 à Ouagadougou, sur la maladie, ses modes de transmission et les moyens de limiter sa propagation. Initiée par le ministère de la Santé, à travers la Direction de la protection de la santé de la population (DPSP), le SP/Palu et le Programme national de lutte contre les maladies tropicales négligées (PNLMTN), la session a mis l’accent sur la communication sur les risques et l’engagement communautaire. Pour les organisateurs, mieux outiller les journalistes doit permettre de renforcer la qualité des messages adressés aux populations. La situation reste suivie de près par les services sanitaires. De la première à la 39e semaine épidémiologique de 2026, 25 780 cas suspects de dengue ont été rapportés, dont 7 226 cas probables et 17 décès. Ces chiffres restent inférieurs à ceux de 2023, année au cours de laquelle le pays avait enregistré 154 867 cas et 709 décès. Des gestes simples contre un risque bien réel La formation a notamment permis de revenir sur le rôle de l’ Aedes aegypti , principal vecteur de la dengue. Contrairement à une idée répandue, ce moustique pique principalement durant la journée, notamment tôt le matin et en fin d’après-midi. Son développement est favorisé par les eaux stagnantes présentes dans différents récipients. Pneus usagés, seaux, bidons, boîtes ou bouteilles peuvent ainsi devenir des gîtes larvaires. La réduction de ces lieux de reproduction constitue donc l’un des premiers moyens de prévention. « Lors de la classification des conteneurs de gîtes larvaires, il est ressorti que les pneus occupent la première place en matière de production de gîtes larvaires, soit de 30 % à plus de 50 % », a expliqué Ousseini Barry, agent de la DPSP. Les participants ont également été sensibilisés aux signes nécessitant une prise en charge rapide, notamment les douleurs abdominales intenses, les vomissements persistants, les saignements, les difficultés respiratoires ou encore une grande fatigue. De l’information à l’action La mobilisation des médias, pour le chef de service de la surveillance épidémiologique, Lassané Kafando, intervient dans un contexte où une hausse des cas est observée depuis la semaine épidémiologique 33. « C’est dans ce cadre que, depuis la semaine épidémiologique 33, nous assistons à une augmentation des cas de dengue au niveau du pays », a-t-il indiqué. Du côté des participants, l’enjeu est désormais de traduire les connaissances acquises en messages accessibles au public. « Nous, en tant que journalistes, ce sont des messages clés que nous devons effectivement transmettre à travers nos écrits, à travers nos émissions » , a souligné Lido Thierno, journaliste à Radio Pulsar. Au-delà de la lutte menée par les services de santé, la prévention de la dengue se joue ainsi aussi dans les habitudes quotidiennes. Éliminer les eaux stagnantes, assainir son environnement et se protéger des piqûres sont autant de gestes qui peuvent contribuer à réduire les risques. Pour les médias, reste désormais le défi de faire de ces réflexes des messages réguliers, compris et surtout appliqués par les populations. Eléonore Savadogo Faso7 L’article Lutte contre la dengue au Burkina Faso : Des professionnels des médias formés pour renforcer la prévention est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: US imposes sanctions on International Criminal Court, hours after Nobel award to former judge
items.description: The United States on Friday imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court, vowing to cripple the tribunal’s operations just hours after the Nobel Peace Prize went to a former ICC judge who warned of mounting political attacks on the court. The move came on the same day the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the peace prize to South Africa’s Navi Pillay, an 85-year-old jurist who headed the Rwanda genocide tribunal, served on the ICC and later led a UN commission that accused Israel of genocide in Gaza. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington would ban transactions with what he called a “rogue court,” escalating a long-running campaign by President Donald Trump’s administration against the Hague-based tribunal. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” Rubio said in a statement, claiming that the court wants more power at the expense of American sovereignty. Rubio’s statement did not mention Pillay or the Nobel award. Instead, he said the sanctions were needed to protect security personnel and elected officials from prosecution by a court the United States has never joined. “President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” Rubio said, adding that the measures would cut off the court’s resources and cripple “its ability to operate”. The top US diplomat said Washington had, for more than a year, spelt out “basic gestures of good faith” it expected from the court, and had held off on the designation in hopes that the ICC or its member states would change course. He said no “meaningful steps” were taken to address US concerns. Rubio also called on US allies that belong to the court and “rely on American service members for their defence” to rein it in, warning that otherwise Washington would keep working to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick”. The Trump administration had previously sanctioned individual ICC officials, including its prosecutor and several judges, over the court’s investigations involving the United States and Israel, which is also not a member. Trump last month called on all ICC member states to quit the body, denouncing it as “out of control” and a “rogue institution. “ The court, however, rejected the US sanctions as an attack on international law and warned in a statement that “history will judge this moment”. In a statement, the court called the sanctions “an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law”. It added that such actions were aimed at intimidating ICC staff and disrupting its activities, vowing it would not be deterred. “The Court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes,” ICC President Tomoko Akane was quoted as saying. The statement called on the ICC’s 125 members to side with the institution, saying: “Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it. “Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an institution created to protect them came under attack,” said the court. States, rights groups back ICC Following the move, several countries and rights groups issued statements condemning US sanctions on the court. The foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Japan and the United Kingdom backed the ICC in a joint statement. “As committed supporters of the ICC, we regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the Court by the United States,” it read. Meanwhile, Amnesty International slammed the US “attack” on the ICC, calling on countries to “resist” after Washington imposed sanctions on the judicial body. President Donald Trump’s “sanctions are designed to isolate and ultimately destroy the International Criminal Court,” Amnesty’s Erika Guevara Rosas said in a statement. “This existential attack must fail. States must take concrete action to resist the imposition of these measures.” UN chief Antonio Guterres condemned Washington’s decision and said he was “deeply alarmed by the expected impact” of the measures. “Today’s decision marks a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar,” his spokesman Stephane Dujarric told reporters. “The secretary-general reiterates his unwavering support for the independence of the Court and its officials,” he added. Similarly, UN human rights chief Volker Turk slammed the new sanctions, saying, “These sanctions — the latest in a series of retaliatory steps against the ICC and its personnel for the work they do every day to advance accountability for the very worst violations of human rights — are unacceptable.” However, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said a six-month pause should be used to pursue negotiations with Washington before the sanctions take effect. “The announced sanctions by the United States against the ICC are deeply regrettable. At the same time, these sanctions will not take effect immediately. And this is crucial because it provides us vital space for dialogue in the upcoming months,” Jetten told reporters.

items.title: Former Deputy Trade and Industry Minister Nana Ama Dokua called to Ghana Bar
items.description: Former Deputy Minister of Trade and Industry Nana Ama Dokua Asiamah-Adjei has been called to the Ghana Bar, marking a new chapter in her professional career nearly two years after stepping away from frontline politics. The former Member of Parliament for Akuapem North was among 1,568 newly qualified lawyers admitted to the legal profession on Friday at a ceremony organised by the General Legal Council in Accra. Her admission comes after a period of relative quiet following the New Patriotic Party’s (NPP) defeat in the December 2024 general elections, bringing renewed attention to the former legislator’s academic pursuits. “Education has no finishing line. My legal training has broadened my understanding of governance, business and people’s rights. It gives me another opportunity to serve society beyond politics,” Asiamah-Adjei said. Since leaving public office in January 2025, she has maintained a relatively low political profile, pursuing legal education away from the national spotlight. Her successful completion of professional legal training represents another milestone in a career spanning business, politics and public administration. Asiamah-Adjei performed particularly well in Evidence, Family Law and Interpretation of Statutes, three important areas of legal education. Her interest in law, however, predates her departure from politics. Parliamentary records from 2017 show that Asiamah-Adjei had enrolled in a distance-learning Bachelor of Laws programme at University College London in 2014, while building her political career. A graduate of the University of Ghana, where she studied psychology and sociology, she also pursued postgraduate studies in logistics and supply chain management at the University of Exeter in the United Kingdom. Before entering Parliament in 2017, she held management positions in several private companies. She represented Akuapem North for two consecutive terms and served as Deputy Minister of Information before becoming Deputy Minister of Trade and Industry under former President Nana Akufo-Addo. Her legal qualification broadens her professional background, particularly in legislation, governance, business regulation and public policy. The former deputy minister joins several prominent public figures admitted to the Bar on Friday, including Communications Minister Samuel Nartey George and Lands and Natural Resources Minister Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah. Her admission opens opportunities for legal practice and other professional engagements, adding a new qualification to more than a decade of experience in public service and business.

items.title: Old Edubiase Methodist Basic School pupils turn traders, farmers as teachers’ strike bites harder
items.description: Classrooms at Old Edubiase Methodist Basic School in the Adansi North District of the Ashanti Region have remained empty for days as pupils abandon their books for farms, markets and football fields following the ongoing nationwide strike by pre-tertiary education teachers. A visit to the community on Thursday, October 8, revealed a disturbing scene of school-going children engaged in all forms of activities except learning. While some pupils were seen accompanying their parents to their cocoa and food crop farms with cutlasses and baskets, others had turned into petty traders, hawking boiled eggs, sachet water and other items along the principal streets of Old Edubiase. Several others were seen loitering around the community, playing football and other games under trees during school hours. In separate interviews, some of the pupils disclosed that their teachers had directed them to stay at home until they are informed that the strike has been called off. “Our teachers told us to stay at home until we hear that the strike has been called off. That is why some of us are doing this,” a Primary Six pupil said. The situation is taking a toll on the pupils who expressed deep unhappiness about the industrial action. “We are not happy with the teachers’ strike because it is having a negative impact on our education. We have been at home for many days doing nothing,” another pupil lamented. The plight of final year students is even more dire. Some Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE) candidates who spoke to this reporter expressed frustration and anxiety as their mock examinations are fast approaching, yet no teaching and learning is ongoing, and no revision has been done. “We are not happy with the teachers’ strike because it has affected our education. Our mock exam is drawing near, and the teachers are on strike. We don’t know what will happen to us,” a BECE candidate, Shadrack Amuzu, said with visible worry. Parents in the community are equally frustrated, as the strike has disrupted both academic work and their daily economic activities. Some parents who were spotted heading to their farms with their children said they had no choice but to send the children to the farm to assist them, while others are left at home unattended. Madam Yaa Nsia, a mother of three whose children are pupils of the school, said the situation has become unbearable. According to her, the strike has forced parents to turn their children into farmhands, while others are just roaming around the community without any supervision. “The strike has forced us to send our children to the farm. Some of the children are just roaming around without going to school because of the strike. This is not good for their future,” she said. She noted that the prolonged closure of schools could expose the children to social vices, teenage pregnancy and child labour. The affected pupils and parents have therefore made a passionate appeal to government and the leadership of the teacher unions to as a matter of urgency, resolve the impasse for academic work to resume. They called on government to listen to the concerns of teachers and address their conditions of service to enable them to return to the classroom. “We are begging the government to listen to our teachers and resolve the issue for them to call off the strike. We want to go back to school,” the pupils appealed. Background Teachers across the country declared a nationwide strike last week over what they describe as the government’s failure to address their conditions of service, including deprived area allowance, promotion issues, and other welfare concerns. The strike has led to a total shutdown of basic schools, with Senior High School also recording low attendance as some parents keep their children at home. The Ghana Education Service (GES) and the Ministry of Education have held several meetings with the teacher unions – Ghana National Association of Teachers (GNAT), National Association of Graduate Teachers (NAGRAT) and Coalition of Concerned Teachers (CCT) – but a breakthrough is yet to be achieved. Meanwhile, residents of Old Edubiase are calling for swift intervention by the Adansi North District Directorate of Education, traditional authorities and government to ensure pupils return to the classroom before irreparable damage is done to the academic calendar.

items.title: Rivers varsity expels final-year student over social media content
items.description: By Davies Iheamnachor The management of Ignatius Ajuru University of Education, Port Harcourt, Rivers State, has expelled a final-year student of the Department of English Language and Literary Studies, Miss Onyewuenyi Chiamaka Nora. This was as the Senate of IAUE announced that the institution has been ranked seventh in staff Google Scholar Profile Submission (by institutions) in the 2026 Ranking of Universities. The Vice-Chancellor of IAUE, Professor Okechuku Onuchuku, made the announcement during the Senate meeting held Wednesday at the Postgraduate Hall, according to an electronic statement by Dr. Ngozi Okiridu, Public Relations Officer of the school. The statement noted that Nora was expelled after her final examination following a disturbing video of her interview with a content creator going viral on social media platforms. In the video, Nora claimed that a lecturer in her department was taking care of her final-year research work and had charged her N150,000 for the job. However, Okiridu, in the statement, said the university deemed the content damaging, adding that the action was to serve as a warning to others. It read: “Senate has expelled Miss Onyewuenyi Chiamaka Nora with Matriculation Number U/2022/19900, a final-year student of the Department of English and Literary Studies, over damaging content creation. The expulsion is to serve as a deterrent to others who may want to do the same. “Recall that the said student had, in an interview that went viral, claimed that her project topic was ‘Citizenship’ when there is no such topic as Citizenship in the Department. She also claimed that her supervisor was the one who wrote the project for her.” On the Google ranking, the statement lauded all academic staff whose articles and publications were cited on Google Scholar, leading to the progress report on Google Scholar Profiles. It thanked staff for giving the university the needed visibility and urged them to sustain the tempo. The post Rivers varsity expels final-year student over social media content appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: The Nobel Laureate Who Rescued Me
items.description: In the winter of 2001, I was in my mid-20s, halfway through a six-year doctoral program in religion that left me uninspired. Friends seemed to be moving forward—in life, in work, in romance. Feeling stuck, I told myself I was taking a leave from graduate school. What this meant was no more lying to myself that I was making progress toward my dissertation (I kept lying to everyone else). Liberated from this pretense, I took a job as a newspaper reporter. I also began auditing an undergraduate poetry class. I’m not sure what inspired me to sit in on this course with Yale undergraduates. Perhaps it was the sheer absurdity of reading and writing poetry with college students as a way into adulthood? In the introductory course on writing verse, we met once a week, read good poems out loud, and wrote bad ones under their inspiration. Our teacher was the celebrated poet J. D. “Sandy” McClatchy. He had a wonderfully resonant baritone, a perfect three-day stubble, and an infectious love of the art form. He told stories about his friendship with James “Jimmy” Merrill , and he would sway his hand in time with the meter of the poems he incanted. When students read their work out loud he gave candid, often brutal criticism. One week Sandy opened his laptop and played a recording of W. H. Auden reading the 1952 poem “ The Shield of Achilles ,” his dystopian take on the scene Hephaestus forges on the shield in The Odyssey . The line about the cruel urchin who’d “never heard / Of any world where promises are kept, / Or one could weep because another wept” stuck me like a blade and brought tears to my eyes. I decided to memorize it. I would memorize a few lines a day. It was difficult at first, then easier. After I had internalized “The Shield of Achilles,” I moved on to Robert Frost’s “ Directive .” Other poems followed. Some I quickly forgot; some became obsessions. For months after memorizing Wallace Stevens’s “Landscape With Boat,” I read it aloud to myself before bed, while listening, always, to Dave Matthews Band’s “ Crush .” I was building a poetry library in bursts, making up for lost time. That is how I came to Anne Carson, the Canadian who won the Nobel Prize for Literature on Thursday. In one of New Haven’s secondhand bookstores, I bought her 2000 collection, Men in the Off Hours , and within it I found her poem “First Chaldaic Oracle.” I’m sure I chose it because it was the one of the shortest in the book. [ Read: Anne Carson’s seductive strangeness ] I knew from the start that I would never understand “First Chaldaic Oracle,” not the way I felt myself to have an understanding of Auden , Frost , or even Stevens , who was weird but on my wavelength. By temperament a square, every once in a while I turn and face the strange, as one weirdo sang , and Anne Carson was my kind of weirdo. I learned “First Chaldaic Oracle” in a matter of days. Here are the first four of the poem’s 10 stanzas: There is something you should know. And the right way to know it is by a cherrying of your mind. Because if you press your mind towards it and try to know that thing as you know a thing, you will not know it. It comes out of red with kills on both sides, it is scrap, it is nightly, it kings your mind. The Chaldean Oracles were lost spiritual texts that survive in fragments in the Neoplatonists’ writings of the third through sixth centuries. So there is a plain reading of the poem at the outset: The “something you should know” may be these unknowable fragments, this “scrap.” But it’s also immediately clear that the poem exists outside of history’s linear accumulation of philosophical knowledge. For what does it mean that “the right way to know it”—whatever “it” is—is not through study, not through religion or archaeology, but “by a cherrying of your mind”? This was the question I got obsessed with: What the hell is a cherrying of the mind? I stopped reading Stevens at night; I let Auden take a back seat. The urgent question was one of cherrying. What was it? Who could do it? Could I cherry my mind? Was that what I needed? The poem has more mysterious irruptions like that. You’ll be going along, reading words that, if we’re honest, are not so far from late-night dorm-room claptrap about the futility of knowing (“try to know,” “you will not know it”), and suddenly the voice turns vatic and omnipotent, powerful enough to invent new verbs: That scrap of knowledge is “nightly, / it kings your mind.” To king —we don’t know what it means, but whatever it is, it’s grand. Then again, squint and we’re on a cosmic chessboard, with nights , homophone to knights . Or is it a checkerboard, where one can be “kinged”? In Carson’s poem, this hard work of knowing, of learning elusive truths, becomes explicitly playful while remaining deadly serious. By the end of the poem, the narrator has given us hope that we can get “it,” the oracular knowledge, the “scrap.” But how? You have to “keep chiselled / keep Praguing the eye // of your soul.” To cherrying, Carson adds “Praguing.” What on earth is “Praguing”?? To unlock the mysteries, one must first solve fresh mysteries. As I understand the poem now, Carson means to teach us new ways to act, new ways to be. New ways to verb the world. Which was exactly what I was looking for that winter. I had tried being a scholar, and I was no good at that. I had tried being a boyfriend, and had been mostly a failure. Friends were in law school or medical school; I was developing no such useful skills. But there was always cherrying and Praguing. I just had to find out what they meant. I could not have articulated this theory of Carson’s “First Chaldaic Oracle” back then, couldn’t have explained why the ultimate futility in the poem’s soul—that I’d never learn to cherry, just as we’d never learn exactly what the Chaldaic oracle said—was so soothing. Somehow this homework assignment from antiquity, as I memorized it, helped unburden me of my ambitions. It freed me. Carson wasn’t there to tell me what to do, but she would at least tell me what not to do. In the middle of the poem, she writes, “The way to know it // is not by staring hard.” And so I didn’t stare hard. I didn’t look for answers. Into the spring, I kept memorizing poems, and I wrote some bad ones of my own. By not “staring hard,” I was able to see what I had to do. I quit my job at the newspaper. I finished my dissertation, after my therapist told me, “This town is filled with people who wish they had.” (My dad also said I’d be glad I did. He was right.) I got a job, got married. I figured out what kind of writer I was supposed to be: a reporter , after all. I just wasn’t ready to embrace that vocation back then. To get there, I needed a little more cherrying and Praguing, whatever that was.
