items.title: WAQF public : le Premier ministre réaffirme le soutien de l’État
items.description: Le Premier ministre, Ahmadou Alhaminou M. Lô, a reçu, ce vendredi 9 octobre 2026, les responsables de la Haute Autorité du WAQF (HAW) pour échanger sur les orientations stratégiques de l’institution et ses projets en cours, notamment la préparation d’un plan stratégique de développement et le lancement prochain du fonds WAQF public. Des orientations pour les dossiers stratégiques La séance de travail a réuni le directeur général de la HAW, Dr Ahmed Lamine Athie, et le président de sa Commission de supervision, El Hadj Amar Lô. Cette rencontre a permis aux responsables de l’institution de recueillir les orientations du chef du gouvernement sur les dossiers stratégiques du WAQF, rattaché à la Primature. Le WAQF est un mécanisme de solidarité durable destiné à mobiliser et à gérer des ressources pour financer des projets sociaux au bénéfice des populations, en particulier les plus vulnérables. À travers ses missions, cette institution publique entend contribuer au renforcement des mécanismes de partage et de soutien aux initiatives sociales. Le fonds WAQF public en préparation Parmi les chantiers en cours figure l’élaboration du plan stratégique de développement de la HAW, ainsi que la mise en place du fonds WAQF public, dont le lancement est annoncé prochainement. Ces initiatives doivent contribuer à structurer l’action de l’institution et à renforcer sa capacité à soutenir des projets à vocation sociale. À l’issue des échanges, le Premier ministre a réitéré son engagement à apporter à la HAW le soutien institutionnel nécessaire à l’accomplissement de ses missions. Un appui destiné à accompagner le développement du WAQF et à consolider son rôle dans la promotion d’une solidarité durable au Sénégal. C.G.D

Reconnu coupable d'escroquerie et d'usurpation d'un titre rattaché à une profession réglementée, le principal prévenu, Mouhamed Coulibaly, a été condamné à un an d’emprisonnement ferme, alors que le procureur avait requis 5 ans de prison. items.title: Tchamba 2 : 100 élèves démunis de l’EPP Ababilé bénéficient de kits scolaires
items.description: Tchamba, 9 oct. (ATOP) – L’ONG Humanity First Togo-Allemagne a distribué, le mercredi 7 octobre, des kits scolaires à 100 élèves démunis de l’Ecole primaire publique (EPP) Ababilé, dans le canton de Koussountou, commune Tchamba 2. Les kits sont composés notamment de cahiers et de sacs. Le geste vise à accompagner les élèves nécessiteux à l’occasion de cette rentrée scolaire 2026-2027 afin qu’ils puissent étudier dans de meilleures conditions. Il s’agit également de soulager les peines des parents d’élèves à majorité dépourvus de moyens. Des donateurs, des enseignements et les bénéficiaires à l’EPP Ababile Le responsable régional de Humanity First Togo-Allemagne du centre, Lamboni Abdul Razzaq, a rappelé que leur organisation apporte des soutiens aux populations défavorisées dans plusieurs domaines, sans distinction aucune. Il a aussi indiqué que ce don vient en appui aux efforts du gouvernement en matière d’éducation de qualité pour tous. Il a invité d’autres donateurs à emboîter leur pas en se rendant dans les hameaux les plus reculés où le besoin se fait sentir. Le directeur de l’EPP Ababilé, Fousséni Assoumanou, a confié que beaucoup d’enfants ont besoin d’aide pour l’achat d’articles scolaires dans la localité. Il a sollicité les bonnes volontés pour la construction des salles de classes modernes. Le directeur a exhorté les parents à mieux encadrer leurs enfants pour un meilleur devenir. Le chef du village d’Ababilé, Simtoga Dada, a déclaré que ce don vient à point nommé apporter le sourire aux élèves. « Avec la cherté de la vie, on n’arrivait pas à acheter toutes les fournitures scolaires. Grâce à leur appui, nos enfants peuvent aller à l’école comme les autres », a-t-il laissé entendre. ATOP/SA/MEK/MD

items.title: Bamako Fashion Week : la mode au service de l’économie
items.description: © Internet Le Mémorial Modibo Keïta a accueilli, le 8 octobre, l’ouverture de la troisième Bamako Fashion Week. Pendant trois jours, l’événement met en avant la création, l’entrepreneuriat culturel et la valorisation des produits locaux. La cérémonie d’ouverture a été marquée par plusieurs séquences consacrées au patrimoine et à l’identité culturelle, notamment le Défilé du Sahel, mettant en lumière la créativité régionale. Placée sous le thème « La mode, levier de développement économique, social, culturel et environnemental », cette troisième édition entend contribuer à la professionnalisation du secteur. L’ouverture du marché des créateurs a également donné lieu à une visite officielle des stands d’exposition. La journée s’est achevée par un cocktail réunissant professionnels de la mode, médias, artisans et public. Les officiels et organisateurs se sont accordés sur la nécessité de transformer les talents en opportunités économiques concrètes. « Notre objectif n’est pas seulement de célébrer la beauté des créations, mais de contribuer à construire un secteur plus fort, dynamique et professionnel, capable de créer de la valeur, des emplois et des perspectives pour notre jeunesse », a déclaré Mariam Bocoum, fondatrice de l’événement. Elle a également plaidé pour une démarche de mode écoresponsable profitant davantage aux communautés locales. Un avis partagé par Mahamadou Diarra dit Koumbouna, secrétaire général du ministère chargé de la Culture. « Le talent à lui seul ne suffit pas toujours. Il doit être accompagné par la formation, la discipline, la professionnalisation et l’innovation », a-t-il insisté. Il a également appelé à renforcer les synergies entre créateurs, investisseurs, institutions et médias. De son côté, le représentant de l’Union européenne au Mali a rappelé que « la mode n’est pas un simple spectacle, elle est également l’affirmation d’une identité au service de l’économie nationale ». Il a aussi mis en avant la place des femmes et des jeunes dans le développement et la professionnalisation du secteur. « La mode raconte qui nous sommes, notre patrimoine, nos influences et notre capacité à réinventer nos traditions pour les inscrire dans la modernité », a, pour sa part, souligné le représentant de Canal+. Le Mali figure parmi les principaux pays producteurs de coton en Afrique et dispose d’une riche tradition textile, notamment autour du bogolan, de l’indigo et du tissage. Mais la transformation locale reste limitée. Selon Mariam Bocoum, « moins de 1 % du coton est actuellement transformé localement », une situation qui, estime-t-elle, ne reflète pas le potentiel de la production nationale. L’un des défis mis en avant au cours de cette édition est donc de mobiliser davantage la jeunesse et les acteurs du secteur afin d’accroître la transformation locale et de mieux valoriser l’ensemble de la chaîne, du producteur de coton au couturier. Historique et perspectives Née en 2011 sous le nom de « Chris Seydou Fashion Week », l’initiative a depuis évolué pour devenir la Bamako Fashion Week. Cette troisième édition entend renforcer son ouverture africaine et internationale et offrir une vitrine aux créateurs, artisans et autres professionnels de la mode malienne. Ali Sankaré

items.title: PDP alleges plot to disrupt PVC collection in Ogun, urges tight security
items.description: By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Ogun State has alleged a plot by the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) to disrupt the ongoing Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) collection exercise, calling on the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) and security agencies to strengthen security at collection centres across the state. In a statement issued on Friday, the PDP said it had received what it described as credible intelligence suggesting plans to deploy suspected thugs to INEC collection centres to intimidate registrants, disrupt the exercise and cart away PVCs belonging to eligible voters. The statement, signed by the party’s Publicity Secretary, Arc. Kayode Adebayo, alleged that the APC was behind the purported plan. According to the opposition party, the alleged plot, if established, would undermine the electoral process and infringe on citizens’ rights to participate freely in elections. The PDP said, “According to reports at our disposal, the ruling APC is allegedly perfecting plans to deploy hired thugs and miscreants to various INEC collection centres with the nefarious objective of disrupting the process, intimidating legitimate registrants, and carting away PVCs belonging to innocent citizens.” The party urged INEC to take proactive measures to protect the collection exercise across Ogun State’s 20 local government areas. “We therefore call on the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to be exceedingly vigilant, proactive, and uncompromising in securing all PVCs and collection centres across the 20 Local Government Areas of Ogun State,” the statement said. It also called on the Nigeria Police Force, the Department of State Services (DSS) and the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) to deploy adequate personnel to collection points and respond promptly to any incidents of intimidation or disruption. The PDP further urged security agencies to investigate suspected acts of electoral interference and prosecute anyone found culpable in accordance with the law. Beyond its appeal to the authorities, the party advised residents to remain vigilant and law-abiding throughout the collection exercise. It cautioned eligible voters against surrendering their PVCs to unauthorised individuals and encouraged them to report suspicious activities to INEC officials or security personnel. “Your PVC is your inalienable right and the potent weapon with which to determine your future,” the party said, adding that voters should not surrender their cards to any individual under any circumstances. The opposition party maintained that no political organisation should interfere with citizens’ constitutional rights to vote, stressing the need for a peaceful and credible electoral process ahead of the 2027 general elections. “The PDP reiterates unequivocally that no political party, no matter how desperate, has the right to interfere with the constitutional right of Nigerians to vote,” the statement added. The party reaffirmed its commitment to what it described as a peaceful, transparent, credible and inclusive electoral process. However, the allegations against the APC were contained in the PDP’s statement, and no independent evidence was provided in the release to establish the existence of the alleged plot. The post PDP alleges plot to disrupt PVC collection in Ogun, urges tight security appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: GHIMA sounds alarm over unlicensed practitioners handling health data, warns of threat to patient safety
items.description: The Ghana Health Information Management Association (GHIMA) has warned against the use of unqualified and unlicensed personnel in managing health information in healthcare facilities. The group says the practice threatens patient safety, the quality of healthcare delivery and the effective implementation of government health policies. The Association says the situation could compromise the accuracy, reliability and timely availability of health data required for clinical decision-making, monitoring healthcare interventions and assessing the effectiveness of government-funded programmes. President of GHIMA, Richard Delali Ahedor, led a press conference to address concerns over professional standards and licensing requirements in Health Information Management (HIM) practice. The Association cited the Health Professions Regulatory Bodies Act, 2013 (Act 857), which mandates the Allied Health Professions Council (AHPC) to regulate, accredit and license allied health professionals, including Health Information Management practitioners. “Under the Health Professions Regulatory Bodies Act, 2013 (Act 857), the Allied Health Professions Council (AHPC) regulates, accredits, and licenses allied health professional practices in Ghana, including our profession (Health Information Management). GHIMA wishes to remind stakeholders that a valid AHPC license is legally required to practice Health Information Management in Ghana.” GHIMA stressed that health information management functions must be performed by qualified and licensed professionals to safeguard the integrity of health data and support effective clinical and policy decisions. “Clinical decisions, health policy, and patient safety depend on accurate health data. HIM functions must, therefore, be performed by practitioners who hold a recognised HIM qualification and a valid AHPC license,” said Mr Ahedor. The Association is urging heads of healthcare facilities and other stakeholders to assign health information management responsibilities to qualified and licensed professionals and support continuous professional development to maintain professional standards. It has also encouraged Health Information Management graduates and practitioners who are yet to obtain certification or licensing to register with the AHPC and complete the required licensing examinations. GHIMA further appealed to the government and healthcare agencies to prioritise the employment and deployment of licensed health information professionals across all levels of healthcare, particularly as the country expands access to healthcare services. The Association says strengthening the profession is critical to generating credible and timely health data to evaluate government policies and guide evidence-based decisions, including the implementation of the Free Primary Healthcare initiative. The maiden General Meeting of GHIMA’s Ashanti Regional Chapter highlighted the shortage of health information officers in some healthcare facilities and the potential implications for health data quality and service delivery. General Secretary of GHIMA, James Amewudah, called on the government to address the situation, warning that the absence of qualified professionals handling health records could undermine the monitoring and evaluation of major healthcare initiatives, including Mahama Care and Free Healthcare. He said accurate health data was essential to determine whether resources invested in such programmes were achieving their intended objectives. “We recognise that all the initiatives that are being run now, for instance, the Mahama Care, free healthcare, they all need to be evaluated and monitored. If we don’t do monitoring and evaluation, resources that are pumped into these initiatives won’t be known if they’ve achieved their purpose or goal or not.” “We need to get the professionals working on the data on health records in order to see if the policies are achieving their purpose,” he said. items.title: Lacs/clôture des activités du projet ACF- AO : Des résultats satisfaisants enregistrés
items.description: Aného, 9 oct. (ATOP)- Un atelier de clôture des activités du projet « Action climatique féministe en Afrique de l’Ouest » (ACF-AO) s’est tenu le jeudi 8 octobre à Aného. La rencontre a permis de faire le bilan de la mise en œuvre du projet, de présenter ses principaux résultats et enseignements et de relever des perspectives pour la consolidation et la pérennisation des acquis au bénéfice des communautés. Ces assises ont été une occasion de valoriser les réalisations et les expériences des bénéficiaires, notamment celles des femmes, des organisations communautaires et des coopératives accompagnées. Des témoignages des bénéficiaires ont été également présentés. Le projet ACF-AO, lancé en avril 2023, est porté par l’Institut africain pour le développement économique et social (INADES-FORMATION) avec l’appui technique et financier des Affaires mondiales Canada (AMC) à travers l’ONG Inter-pares. Il est mis en œuvre dans les communes Lacs 1, 2 et 4 et Vo 2. L’objectif est de contribuer au renforcement de la résilience des communautés côtières et aux changements climatiques en mettant l’accent sur la restauration et la gestion durable des écosystèmes, le renforcement du leadership et du pouvoir économique des femmes, la promotion des pratiques agroécologiques et de la pêche durable. Fondé sur une approche participative, le projet ACF-AO a touché environ 10 500 bénéficiaires directs, dont 78 % de femmes. En termes de renforcement des capacités et d’appui technique, 2478 personnes ont été formées sur la participation des femmes et des jeunes aux instances de décision et 604 renforcées sur le plaidoyer. 3758 acteurs sont formés sur les politiques climatiques, la biodiversité et le genre, 3337 sensibilisés à l’adaptation et à l’atténuation et 1542 autres formés en développement des affaires, gestion des coopératives, chaînes de valeurs et mise en marché. Le représentant du ministre en charge de l’Environnement, M. Dossou Kodjo, a souligné que la clôture de ce projet doit ouvrir une nouvelle phase, celle de l’appropriation, de la consolidation et de la pérennisation des acquis. Il a formulé le vœu que les acquis de cette expérience continuent de produire des effets durables dans les communes concernées et qu’ils puissent inspirer d’autres initiatives à travers le pays. « Vous nous rappelez que protéger les mangroves, restaurer les écosystèmes ou renforcer les économies locales, c’est aussi une façon de bâtir la justice sociale et un monde plus égal », a indiqué le chargé de programme de l’Inter Pares, Mme Abanda Ngongo Fernande. La rencontre a pris fin par la visite des stands de l’exposition des produits agricoles promus par le projet. Cet évènement a mobilisé des autorités administratives, traditionnelles, des élus locaux, des coopératives et organisations de la société civile, des représentants des services techniques et des partenaires. ATOP/DK/MD

items.title: FO says Pakistan has 'substantial number of forces, resources' in Riyadh
items.description: Foreign Office (FO) spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said on Friday that Pakistan already had “substantial number” of forces and resources in Riyadh and it was now up to the Makkah Defence Alliance to assess the threat in Saudi Arabia and make decisions accordingly. The FO spokesperson remarks came in response to a query about the “active support” being offered by Pakistan to Saudi Arabia under the Makkah Defence Alliance amid an escalating conflict between the kingdom and Yemen-based Houthis. The Makkah Defence Alliance is a tripartite arrangement that includes Turkiye as well. It was signed on Aug 7 and and aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. Speaking during a weekly briefing, the FO spokesperson recalled that a joint statement by the three members of the alliance was “very clear in stating that the three countries are united in ensuring deterrence and safeguarding the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia”. The three countries had decided to contribute and mobilise resources rapidly, he said, adding that Pakistan already had a “substantial number of forces, as well as resources, in Riyadh”. “It is now up to the organisation to assess the threat perception and operate in accordance with its own mandate,” he said. The spokesperson went on to say that providing further details on operational matters of the alliance, “including how the situation will be handled, would not be appropriate on my part. It would also be speculative on my part to suggest that certain countries could be involved”. On the Houthis and escalation of the conflict, he said, “This is a militia that has been involved in such proxy activities and has contributed to regional instability. It has been actively fighting Yemeni forces for quite some time, and access to resources is possible these days. However, at this stage, I would not be able to provide you with specific names”. Yemen’s civil war has rapidly emerged as the fiercest front in a wider regional conflagration triggered by the US and Israeli attack on Iran that started on February 28. Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said on Friday that three Saudi nationals ​were killed and several people were injured in ‌two attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Thursday. The strikes, which also injured several people, damaged a Saudia Airlines plane and sent smoke billowing over the airport, led many airlines to cancel flights to the Saudi capital days before it is due to host a major meeting of global oil chiefs. Saudi airstrikes hit Houthi targets in the Yemeni capital Sanaa overnight, Houthi officials and affiliated media said, part of an intensifying air war against the Iran-allied group aimed at reversing its recent territorial ​gains, threats to international shipping, and attacks on the kingdom. The Yemeni group says it is targeting the kingdom over its support for government forces in Yemen’s reignited civil war. Saudi Arabia says it is backing ​an offensive by ​Yemen’s UN-recognised ⁠government to take back territory from the Houthis. Pakistan role, as part of the Makkah defence pact, has been a matter of discussion against this backdrop. While Pakistan has expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia, it has also maintained that the Makkah alliance is intended for collective deterrence and defensive in nature. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Friday condemned recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, reiterating Pakistan’s commitment to the Gulf state’s “sovereignty, territorial integrity and security” under the Makkah Defence Alliance. A day ago, the Ministry of Information dismissed on Thursday a news report claiming that Pakistan Air Force aircraft were being used against the Yemen’s Houthis as “fake and fabricated”. Earlier this week, the ministry also termed a Reuters report claiming the deployment of 30,000 to 40,000 Pakistani troops in Saudi Arabia as “speculative”. Nevertheless, on Monday, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye agreed to the deployment of military forces and capabilities rapidly in the kingdom during an emergency meeting of the Makkah Defence Alliance in Riyadh. Monday’s meeting under the alliance was held to address the security developments and threats facing Saudi Arabia. A statement issued by the Foreign Office after the meeting said the member states had “decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom, in accordance with the approved arrangements and the national legislation of the parties, thereby enhancing readiness, military integration, and the collective capacity to confront and counter threats”. Separately, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, who was part of Pakistan’s delegation in the meeting, joined Geo News programme ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Saath’ via telephone the same day and said Pakistan and Turkiye, the defence minister replied that both nations had a “presence in theatre”, but only Saudi troops were involved in combat operations. He also said on Thursday that no stipulation of the Makkah Defence Alliance barred the member states from getting “directly involved” in case of a threat to one of the members. Moscow Format meeting The FO spokesperson also addressed the reason for the lack of a joint statement issued after the Moscow Format meeting, saying that it was due to the Afghan Taliban delegation’s departure from its previous position regarding the language on terrorism. He noted that Pakistan had participated constructively in the meeting and “clearly conveyed its concerns” about terrorism emanating from Afghan territory, underscoring that it posed a serious threat to neighbouring countries. “As you are aware, these concerns were duly reflected in the joint statement issued at last year’s Moscow Format meeting,” Khan said. “However, this year, the Afghan Taliban delegation did not agree to retain the previously agreed language and departed from its earlier position.” He added, “We believe that any joint statement that does not adequately reflect this legitimate security concern would not present a fair picture of the ground realities. For Pakistan, this is a substantive security issue, not merely a matter of wording.” However, the spokesperson highlighted that “the absence of a joint statement should not overshadow the value of regional dialogue”. He added that Pakistan had sufficient time to hold consultations regarding future participation in the Moscow Format, as the next meeting was a year away. “As I have already mentioned, that is part of our engagement on the issue, and possibly we might continue to participate in the future as well,” he said, although he ruled out making any definitive commitments as “premature”. New map issued by India Additionally, the FO rejected the issuance of a new political map by India in which parts of India-occupied Jammu and Kashmir were depicted as a part of Indian territorial jurisdiction, terming it an “act of cartographic aggression” and noting that it did not make India’s occupation legitimate. “Pakistan categorically rejects India’s latest act of cartographic aggression,” Khan said while answering a question. He added, “Any motivated and unilateral cartographic exercise is legally void and in clear violation of the relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions. Such illegal actions cannot confer legitimacy on India’s occupation of large parts of Jammu and Kashmir.” Noting that unilateral action by India could not alter the internationally-recognised disputed status of the region, he further said that these measures could not “prejudice the inalienable right of the Kashmiri people to self-determination”, which should be exercised via a free and impartial plebiscite under UN auspices. “Instead of resorting to futile cartographic exercises, India must abide by international law, fulfill its obligations under the relevant UN Security Council resolutions, and allow the people of illegally occupied Jammu and Kashmir to exercise their right to self-determination,” the spokesperson added.

items.title: RSF preps new front from Ethiopia, pummels Blue Nile; In Kordofan, RSF conducts ‘field’ executions, digs in heels at Nuhud; Dagris prison dispute stalls registry; Gov’t criticizes UN fact-finding renewal
items.description: Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . With all eyes turned toward the escalating conflict in Ethiopia that is teetering on the brink of becoming a wider regional war, the Rapid Support Forces stepped up their attacks on the Sudan war’s southeastern front this week. Blue Nile’s Wad al-Mahi locality in the east of the state bore the brunt of the escalation. The RSF launched an attack from Ethiopia on Saturday and seized the Kadalo mountains area, which sits near the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and Roseires Dam reservoir. This coincided with a drone campaign against Damazin, which included strikes on the homes of Blue Nile Governor Ahmed Badry and Regional Finance Minister Abbas Kara, fuel stations, military sites, universities and mosques. The military has hit back, launching airstrikes on RSF positions in Wad al-Mahi and tried to reassure residents. As of Sunday, about 2,800 people are estimated to have been displaced from 10 villages in Wad al-Mahi. But action in the southeastern front wasn’t limited to the Blue Nile. Large numbers of RSF fighters have been moved from Darfur to Addis Ababa in recent weeks in preparation to transfer them toward Sudan’s eastern border, where they are expected to gear up for an attack on the Fashaga border strip in Gadarif State, according to an RSF source and another source informed of the mobilization arrangements who spoke to Mada Masr. In anticipation of escalating attacks on the border, the Sudanese military has reinforced its positions in the east, military sources tell Mada Masr. And on Wednesday, military chief and Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan visited the 11th Infantry Division in Khashm al-Gerba, Kassala State, which borders Gadarif to the north. On the western front, the military is preparing to attack the remaining RSF-held areas in North Kordofan and advance into West Kordofan, with eyes set on Um Bader and Hamra al-Sheikh in northwestern North Kordofan. Meanwhile, the RSF is digging its heels in West Kordofan, with the group having dug trenches and built earth berms around the strategic city of Nuhud to guard against surprise attacks, an activist in the state told Mada Masr. West Kordofan also saw yet another attack on an aid truck this week, with Khartoum laying blame for the strike at the feet of the RSF and the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (Abdel Aziz al-Hilu faction). In Um Bader, a social media video of the execution of 23 detainees is raising concern. While the RSF-led Tasis government tried to pin the executions on the military, three sources from the paramilitary group confirmed that the RSF had carried out the ‘field’ executions. As to why, the RSF sources’ accounts conflicted with those of medical sources and relatives of one of the men killed who spoke to Mada Masr. But both Tasis and officials in Khartoum are keen to pursue justice, even if a Tasis official continued to dismiss the RSF’s implications when presented with what sources from the paramilitary told Mada Masr. In Darfur, the joint forces push toward Geneina continues to stall, with territory swapping hands. The US’s politicking over the Darfur arms embargo — which has done next to nothing to stop the flow of weapons through Darfur or seen the provider of those arms in the United Arab Emirates face international criticism — got kicked down the road for another two months, as DC continues its push to extend the embargo across the whole country. The UN’s fact-finding committee on Sudan did get its mandate renewed, much to the chagrin of the government in Khartoum, which sees any form of international intervention as an infringement on its sovereignty. And opacity around the infamous Dagris prison, where an estimated 20,000 people are being detained, has posed a roadblock in the government-RSF prisoner exchange registry process. In yet another senior defection from the paramilitary group, Mohamed Azrag al-Fanjary, the commander of an RSF special operations group, announced on Thursday that he and around 300 officers and soldiers with 30 combat vehicles would join the military. You can read all about how the defections are symptomatic of a larger contradiction at the core of the RSF project in a Mada Masr investigation published earlier this week. *** RSF executes 23 detainees in North Kordofan’s Um Bader, sources say RSF troops prepare to shoot a group of blindfolded men in Um Bader in North Kordofan, September 24. Courtesy: Journalist Ahmed Albalal via X. Twenty-three people were executed in the RSF-held town of Um Bader in western North Kordofan on September 24 after being detained by the paramilitary group, according to three RSF sources, a medical source, a source with the military-allied joint force and a relative of one of the 23. All of them agree that the RSF executed the group, but their accounts differ over their affiliation, what they had been accused of and what happened before they were killed. The killings follow a longstanding pattern of violence and reprisals in the area, which has intensified since the military launched its campaign across the state in July. The RSF forces operating along this axis are commanded by Abdel Rahman Jumaa Barakallah, who was sanctioned by the UN Security Council for human rights abuses committed while commanding RSF forces in West Darfur in 2023. A video circulating over the past week shows the execution. A group of blindfolded men are made to lie face down with their hands bound behind their backs as armed men in RSF uniforms stand near them. The person filming the video says the men had looted Um Bader’s market and identifies an RSF field commander, Ali al-Balla Gabbara, as being in charge of the execution. The men are ordered shot in groups. The RSF-led Tasis alliance, which heads the parallel government in western Sudan, sought to distance itself from the incident on October 2, saying the group was killed by the military and its allies in Sodary, a town captured by the military the previous week. In a statement, Tasis accused the forces of carrying out a “heinous massacre,” saying they executed “innocent citizens in cold blood in a public square” after taking control of Sodary, on the pretext that they had stolen from the markets. But accounts from multiple sides confirm Um Bader as the site of the killings. Mutawakkel Abu Gaa, the spokesperson for the military-allied joint force, confirmed to Mada Masr that the 23 civilians were killed there by the RSF, citing information the force received from the area. A RSF source likewise confirmed that an execution was carried out by the group, saying the victims were killed at Jabal Um Bader, north of the town, in the presence of RSF military police officers. The source said the bodies were later buried in a mass grave near the site. The circumstances surrounding their detention remain contested. According to a source in the Sudan Doctors Network, the 23 had been held in RSF custody after being accused of siding with the military and of theft — charges the source said were also driven by ethnic bias. Some of those detained denied the accusations and demanded a trial, according to information gathered by the medical group. A relative of one of the men told Mada Masr that his family has been trying to establish what happened to him. Several families, he said, have been searching for their relatives since the incident and maintain that the men had no ties to either the RSF or the military. He said they were civilians who worked in the gold market. Two RSF sources disputed that account. They said the group had arrived in Um Bader from Nyala, in South Darfur, and had been detained after committing thefts and killing civilians. They said an internal investigation found them to be affiliated with the RSF, after which they were subjected to a “field trial” that ended in their execution. A source in the Tasis government said the administration was prepared to open an investigation if evidence emerged of RSF involvement, dismissing the accounts provided by the RSF sources to Mada Masr as unreliable, and saying Tasis would summon the commander of the Um Bader force. So far, however, the evidence available points to RSF involvement in both detaining the group and killing its members, based on corroborating accounts from the field, an informed judicial source with Khartoum state authorities, who is based in North Kordofan, told Mada Masr. Whatever the circumstances of their detention, killing people in custody constitutes a grave breach of international humanitarian law, the source added. The law prohibits the killing of detainees and people who are no longer taking part in hostilities outside of the scope of judicial proceedings. State investigators are now documenting the incident, working to identify the victims and establish the chain of command behind the killings — including who carried them out and who ordered them — before determining criminal responsibility on the basis of the evidence, he said. The Um Bader killings came against a backdrop of repeated violence across western North Kordofan. Over the past months, in Murra, Um Saadoun, Rada, Um Kiredam, Shag al-Nom and elsewhere, civilians have been killed, wounded, displaced from their homes and had their property looted, according to a source in North Kordofan state government appointed by Khartoum who spoke to Mada Masr. Local authorities have attributed the incidents to RSF forces deployed across the area. Information gathered by the state government on RSF troop deployments places the units involved within the command of Abdel Rahman Jumaa Barakallah, the source said. Barakallah took charge of the area after the RSF’s withdrawal from Khartoum in early 2025. He had initially been appointed commander of the group’s Omdurman sector, which borders North Kordofan. But after the RSF was driven from Omdurman weeks later, he was reassigned to North Kordofan, a former member of the RSF’s operations authority in North Kordofan, who defected to the military, told Mada Masr. From there, he remained responsible for the commanders leading operations on the North Kordofan and West Bara axis. The RSF’s presence in the area came under increasing pressure in July, when the military launched a sweeping campaign against its strongholds across North Kordofan. The military captured Bara, Um Sayala and Gabra al-Sheikh, among other areas, forcing the RSF to fall back toward positions in the West Bara and Sodary localities. The withdrawal was followed by a new wave of retaliatory attacks, according to a notable from the Majaneen tribe, whose nazirate is based in Mazroub, which was under RSF control until last week. The attacks struck Mazroub, Um Bader, Sodary, Abu Zaeima and Hamra al-Sheikh, the tribal notable said, with withdrawing RSF forces looting markets and homes and detaining dozens of residents accused of passing information to the military. The Sudan Doctors Network accused the RSF of killing at least five civilians and displacing thousands of residents in attacks across West Bara between July 25 and 26, as forces withdrawing from Bara redeployed through the area. Barakallah’s responsibility for the axis carries added significance because of his earlier record in West Darfur, where he commanded RSF forces during some of the war’s worst violence. The UN Security Council sanctioned Barakallah in November 2024, identifying him as an RSF major general and commander of the group’s forces in West Darfur. The council said he was listed over acts and policies threatening peace, security and stability in Darfur, including violence and human rights abuses. It also linked him to the killing of West Darfur governor Khamis Abakar, who was last seen in Barakallah’s company before his death, as well as to RSF and allied attacks in Geneina and Ardamata that killed thousands of people. *** Khartoum presses Red Cross on detainee exchange, RSF’s Dagris prison at center of registry challenges Sudan’s Foreign Ministry has asked the International Committee of the Red Cross to step up its work on the exchange of civilian and military detainees held by the Sudanese military and the RSF, as the government works to build a verified registry of people held by the two sides. The RSF’s Dagris prison in Nyala, where the government estimates that more than 20,000 people are being held, has emerged as one of the most difficult parts of that effort, according to sources in the government, with little access to the facility and limited information available about many of those detained there. The request came during an October 2 meeting between Deputy Foreign Minister Muawiya Othman Khaled, who was in New York for the UN General Assembly, and Elyse Nicole Mosquini, the head of the ICRC’s New York office. The meeting focused on moving the detainee file beyond scattered humanitarian contacts toward a more structured process for identifying detainees, verifying their whereabouts and conditions, releasing civilians and arranging the exchange of military prisoners, according to a Foreign Ministry source who spoke to Mada Masr. The government’s push to compile a registry followed a June proposal by Pekka Haavisto, the UN secretary-general’s personal envoy for Sudan, to work toward a prisoner exchange in coordination with the ICRC. In July, the TSC established a preparatory committee tasked with compiling and verifying detainee lists and called on families who had not previously reported detained or missing relatives to register their cases. Senior sources from both the military and the RSF told Mada Masr at the time that they supported the proposal on humanitarian grounds, while stressing that any exchange would require internationally monitored safeguards against military manipulation. For the government, the ICRC could provide a channel through which the parties can exchange information about detainees, their places of detention and their conditions, the Foreign Ministry source said. A TSC source said the government is seeking to know the fate of people the RSF transferred from areas it previously controlled in Khartoum, Gezira, Sennar and White Nile states to Darfur. Families have often been unable to reach the detention sites and, in some cases, have lost contact with their relatives altogether, the source added. Dagris is the largest known detention site in that network. A government source serving on the preparatory committee estimates that more than 20,500 people are held there and in surrounding military garrisons, including members of the armed forces, police and intelligence services, civilians, medical workers and women. The estimate includes 5,000 civilians transferred from Fasher, 3,795 members of the armed forces, 4,670 police officers, 564 intelligence personnel, 83 medical workers and 720 women, the source said. The number could grow as families continue to report missing relatives and receive information about people inside the prison through intermediaries. The figures cannot be independently verified. Human rights and humanitarian organizations have been unable to gain access to Dagris, according to a human rights source monitoring detainees in Darfur. Accounts collected from former detainees and families of people still being held point to sharply deteriorating conditions, including shortages of food, water and medical care, the source said. The Committee for Justice, a Geneva-based human rights organization, documented the deaths of more than 215 detainees at Dagris in May and June. It attributed the deaths to what it described as deteriorating detention conditions and the spread of disease, and reported repeated allegations of ill-treatment and denial of medical care. In May, the committee also documented what it described as a “troubling pattern” in which civilian detainees were released after their families paid money. The organization said the cases amount to exploitation of families’ suffering. As for their legal status, some detainees have spent prolonged periods in custody without their families receiving clear information about the charges against them or the judicial proceedings, the human rights source said. For rights groups, those concerns mean that any future exchange would need to go beyond compiling names. It would require an independent mechanism to verify detainees’ conditions, gain access to detention sites, document deaths in custody and establish the fate of people whose whereabouts remain unknown, the source said. Dagris makes humanitarian access and independent monitoring an essential part of any process for dealing with detainees and prisoners, the source added. *** New attack on WFP aid convoy in South Kordofan A World Food Programme convoy of aid trucks were hit by an airstrike on Saturday while traveling between Dalang and Kadugli in South Kordofan. The trucks were “clearly marked as humanitarian vehicles,” according to the WFP, which called for an independent investigation to identify those responsible and hold them accountable. Two government sources, one in the Foreign Ministry and the other in the South Kordofan administration, told Mada Masr that the strike was carried out by the RSF and its ally the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu, citing investigation findings and information the authorities had received. In a statement condemning the strike, the United Nations Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown, noted that the convoy, which she said was carrying lifesaving assistance, was hit in an area “that has been under continued attack by the RSF and the SPLM-N.” The attack took place along the same route where two WFP trucks carrying food aid to Kadugli were struck outside Dalang just weeks before. The latest convoy was hit by the allies’ drones, killing one driver and injuring others, the source in the state government said. Two trucks were damaged, he added. Humanitarian shipments between cities in South Kordofan rely heavily on road transport, making the Dalang-Kadugli road a crucial route for moving food and other supplies, the source said. Local authorities are trying to secure convoy movements, he added, but threats linked to fighting, shelling and drone attacks have made such efforts an increasingly complex task. Drivers now weigh the threat before every trip. One who regularly uses the Dalang-Kadugli road told Mada Masr that drivers now assess the situation before setting out, exchanging information about clashes, military movements and conditions along the route. Those conditions can change quickly, he said, sometimes forcing drivers to delay or reschedule journeys. The danger is not confined to areas of direct fighting, the driver added. Vehicles can come under shelling or attack while passing through areas that appear far from the frontlines. The recurrent attacks on aid trucks have raised the stakes for transport workers more broadly, the driver said. The killing of one driver sends a message of fear to everyone who relies on the same routes to move food, fuel and other essential goods between South Kordofan’s cities. The attack on the WFP trucks comes as fighting and restricted access leave roads as a critical lifeline for communities across the state, particularly as local markets in conflict-affected areas become less able to provide basic goods. Targeting these roads also drives up the cost of aid and commercial goods, with organizations and traders paying more to secure vehicles and staff and to reroute convoys. *** UN’s Sudan fact finding mission renewed, Darfur arms embargo extended for 2 months The international investigation into abuses committed during Sudan’s war will continue for another year after the UN Human Rights Council voted on Monday to renew the mandate of its independent fact-finding mission, with 28 countries voting in favor, 10 against and nine abstaining. The renewal put the council again at odds with Sudan’s government, which has argued that accountability for crimes committed during the war should remain primarily in the hands of national institutions. Khartoum has also objected to what it sees as the mission’s tendency to place the Sudanese military and the RSF on the same legal and political footing. The resolution nonetheless draws a distinction on one issue the Sudanese government has made central. It calls for respect for Sudan’s unity and territorial integrity and rejects attempts to establish a parallel governing authority in areas controlled by the RSF. At the same time, it condemns military support to all warring parties and holds both sides responsible for violations committed during the war. The renewal comes as international attention has increasingly focused on the role of drones in expanding the war’s impact on civilians. In its latest report, released September 1 and titled “Fueling Sudan’s conflict: weapons, fighters and external support networks,” the fact-finding mission documented drone attacks by both sides and said their growing range and operational capabilities had allowed the military and RSF to strike far beyond the frontlines, including in places where civilians had sought refuge. “Drone warfare conducted by both the RSF and the Sudanese Armed Forces has extended the geographical reach of hostilities,” the United Kingdom representative said in presenting the draft resolution on Monday. The UK, which led the group of countries behind the resolution, defended the mission as “the only independent investigative body documenting and reporting on these violations and abuses across Sudan,” the representative said. He also sought to answer Sudan’s objections by pointing to the negotiations over the text. “We have held consultations and discussed this draft extensively with all delegations, starting with Sudan,” he said, adding that the sponsors had incorporated a number of proposals from the Sudanese side. “Yet, despite our best efforts, it is regretful that these changes were not enough for the Sudanese authorities.” During the negotiations, the Sudanese delegation argued that the mandate itself should not be extended and that investigations and accountability should remain primarily within the jurisdiction of national institutions, according to a source in the Sudanese mission in Geneva who spoke to Mada Masr. The delegation also objected to what it viewed as an equivalence between the military and the RSF, the source said, and argued that the mission has consistently disregarded abuses attributed to the RSF in several parts of the country. A Foreign Ministry source likewise framed the disagreement as one of sovereignty, saying the government sees the resolution as reflecting the position of some countries that treat the military and RSF as equivalent parties despite their different constitutional and legal status. Khartoum does not oppose international cooperation, the source said, but wants it to operate alongside Sudanese institutions rather than in ways that supersede them. The ministry will continue engaging with states and international organizations over the war, the source added, particularly on the role of external actors in sustaining the flow of weapons, fighters and military support into Sudan. That distinction — between international involvement and international jurisdiction — was echoed by Sudan’s judicial institutions. The Public Prosecution maintains that crimes committed during the war should be investigated and prosecuted by national courts, while allowing international cooperation where cases require the exchange of evidence or information, a source in the Sudanese prosecution told Mada Masr. The prosecution is collecting and documenting reports of violations, the source said, but the existence of an international fact-finding mechanism does not remove the jurisdiction of Sudanese courts over crimes within their remit. For the prosecution, documentation and criminal accountability are separate stages. Establishing individual responsibility requires verifiable evidence linking specific people to crimes, whether as direct perpetrators, those who issued orders or others who contributed to their commission, the source said. International findings can therefore contribute to the evidentiary record, he added, but insisted that they do not by themselves constitute a judicial determination of criminal responsibility. The Justice Ministry similarly regards the council’s resolution as an international political and human rights decision whose implementation inside Sudan remains subject to national law and the jurisdiction of state institutions, a ministry source told Mada Masr. International investigations and accountability mechanisms should operate in complementarity with those institutions, while investigations should cover violations by all parties without exception or selectivity, the source stressed. The government will review the resolution’s recommendations in light of those principles, the source added. Egypt and Qatar were among those voting against the resolution, echoing Sudan’s objections over the treatment of the two sides and the extension of the mission’s mandate. Egypt’s representative told the council that equating the Sudanese military with the RSF sends “the wrong political message at a time when Sudan needs safeguarding its unity.” He also objected to extending the mandate despite what he described as “the non-consent of the concerned country,” and called instead for greater cooperation between the Sudanese government and UN human rights mechanisms. Qatar similarly reaffirmed its support for Sudan’s unity and territorial integrity, while condemning violations committed during the war and foreign interference. Its representative said Qatar rejected equating “an illegal militia with a legitimate, recognized government.” The fact-finding mission was established by the Human Rights Council in October 2023, months after the war began, to investigate the human rights and humanitarian crisis. Its mandate includes identifying individuals and entities responsible for human rights abuses and violations of international humanitarian law, with the aim of supporting accountability and access to justice for victims. A US push to bring drones acquired by all parties to the war, including the Sudanese state, under a nationwide arms embargo has faltered for a second time on Thursday, as Russia and China continued to oppose expanding the existing restrictions beyond Darfur. The UN Security Council instead voted unanimously to extend the Darfur arms embargo until December 11, following the expiry of a one-month technical rollover. The extension had been expected to give Washington more time to lobby council members and negotiate changes, after the initial draft failed to secure the votes needed without risking a Russian veto, an informed UN source told Mada Masr at the time. US Senior Advisor on African and Arab Affairs Massad Boulos said Washington’s decision to support the second rollover does not constitute “a lapse in our resolve.” Boulous stressed that Washington remains committed to expanding the embargo. Khartoum has staunchly opposed the US proposal on the grounds that it equates state institutions with a militia. *** RSF eyes new front in eastern Sudan as military reinforces positions, sources say Military chief and Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan visits the 11th Infantry Division in Kassala, October 7. Courtesy: The TSC. Large numbers of RSF fighters have been moved from Darfur to Addis Ababa as preparations begin to transfer them toward Sudan’s eastern border, where they are expected to prepare for an attack on the Fashaga border strip in Gadarif State, according to an RSF source and another source informed of the arrangements for moving the fighters who spoke to Mada Masr. The RSF source said specialized drone units are among the forces currently undergoing training in Addis Ababa. During his unannounced visit to Addis Ababa in August, RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo delegated a number of RSF leaders to follow the forces’ situation on the ground and make operational decisions, the source added. Over the past week, hundreds of fighters were moved from Darfur to Addis Ababa via an air bridge from Nyala and then transferred to areas near Fashaga in Gadarif, according to the source informed of the transfer operation. The movements are intended to open a new front toward Gadarif, the source said, potentially allowing the RSF, which already controls significant areas in the bordering Blue Nile region, to push deeper into other parts of eastern Sudan. Such a move would be highly sensitive given Fashaga’s strategic location along Sudan’s border with Ethiopia and its proximity to Eritrea, the source warned, and could open the door to a wider escalation along the Sudan-Ethiopia border. The region is already facing a particularly complex security environment, with fighting intensifying between Ethiopia’s federal government and opposition forces in the north, including in Tigray , which borders Sudan, while diplomatic tensions between Addis Ababa and Asmara continue to mount. At the same time, Sudan’s Blue Nile region remains one of the key flashpoints in the country’s civil war, with the RSF and its allies fighting there and with Ethiopia playing a significant role in the movement of military supplies to them. The Sudanese military has been responding to this web of threats by reinforcing its positions in the east. On Wednesday, military chief and Transitional Sovereignty Council chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan visited the 11th Infantry Division in Khashm al-Gerba, Kassala State, which borders Gadarif to the north, “to review the overall security and operational situation in the area,” according to a military statement. Over the past week, the armed forces have sent additional troops to a number of positions in Gadarif and Kassala, part of broader security measures involving military divisions and units across eastern Sudan, according to a military source in the Second Infantry Division in Gadarif. Commanders across both states have been instructed to raise readiness and prepare for any developments along the border, the source said. Military commanders are coordinating on border surveillance and the protection of key facilities and strategic sites, with particular attention to Fashaga and Khashm al-Gerba, as well as the Upper Atbara and Setit Dam Complex on the Tekeze River, near the Ethiopian border, and Wad Zayed Airport, in Gadarif, according to the source. The airport has been undergoing expansion since the beginning of the year as the armed forces seek to strengthen aerial surveillance in Gadarif, and has recently received reinforcements, the source added. A senior Sudanese military officer, who spoke to Mada Masr, maintained that the border on the Gadarif side was fully secured, stressing that the military has strengthened its presence in the area over the past several months. He added that Popular Resistance forces — civilians who volunteer to fight alongside the military — have received advanced training to respond to any potential attack. *** RSF expands in eastern Blue Nile, launches drone campaign on Damazin Aftermath of an RSF drone attack on Damazin in Blue Nile, October 3. Courtesy: Press Office of the Governor of Blue Nile via Facebook. The RSF advanced into a new locality in Blue Nile on the Ethiopian border, expanding its ground offensive in the region, which coincided with a wave of drone strikes on officials’ homes and civilian infrastructure in the regional capital Damazin. On Saturday, RSF troops , including fighters under the command of Obeid Mohamed “Abu Shotal” Solaiman, who hails from Blue Nile, seized the Kadalo mountains area in Wad al-Mahi locality in eastern Blue Nile after launching an attack from inside Ethiopia, a military source told Mada Masr. The area includes the villages of Jabal al-Nimr, Bashkarkad and Minza al-Nimr along the Ethiopian border. The attacking forces had amassed large numbers of fighters inside Ethiopian territory before advancing on military positions under heavy drone cover and taking control of the area, the military source said. The military responded by deploying an additional brigade to Balgwa south of Roseires town to secure the eastern axis and halt their advance, he added. The Kadalo mountains are strategically important because of their location along the Ethiopian border, near the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and the expanded reservoir of the Roseires Dam. The area also is also home to the Dinder National Park and has substantial mineral deposits and extensive agricultural land. The advance displaced thousands of families amid severe shortages of shelter, food and medicine. The International Organization for Migration said that 2,800 people were displaced on Sunday from 10 villages in Wad al-Mahi as the security situation deteriorated. The military has since stepped up its response along the eastern axis. Airstrikes against RSF concentrations intensified, with the heaviest attack coming on Tuesday in Abu Gaddaf , also in Wad al-Mahi, where the air force destroyed 12 combat vehicles and killed several fighters, according to the military source. Some fighters withdrew toward Makla , the source added. The Fourth Infantry Division in Damazin sought to reassure residents, saying the RSF was attempting to create anxiety and uncertainty by spreading “rumors” and exaggerating events. Reinforcement and support forces were on full alert to protect civilians and respond to threats, it said. The ground offensive in Wad al-Mahi coincided with the start of a drone campaign against Damazin. The RSF began targeting the regional capital on Saturday, striking the home of Blue Nile Governor Ahmed Badry. The house was damaged, but no casualties were reported, an official in Blue Nile told Mada Masr. Fuel stations and other civilian and military sites were also hit, the official said. The attacks continued over the week, targeting government officials’ homes and civilian infrastructure. At around 1 am on Wednesday, RSF drones struck the Hijra neighborhood and Sudan Technical College, damaging classrooms, administrative offices and labs. A mosque was destroyed and the headquarters of the Islamic Appeal Organization ’s branch came under fire, according to a medical source and a resident in Damazin who spoke to Mada Masr. Regional Finance Minister Abbas Kara, meanwhile, survived a simultaneous strike on his home along with his family and security detail, the two sources said. Kara said in a statement that his house had been hit four times by an RSF strategic drone, but that no one was injured. The Wednesday attacks killed four civilians and wounded 12. In a statement issued on the same day, the Blue Nile governor described the attacks as a systematic campaign against the region’s residents and “a blatant assault on their lives and security.” Targeting civilians and the families of officials and political leaders, and terrorizing people in their homes “would not achieve the aggressors’ aims or weaken the resolve of the people of Blue Nile,” he said. A former military officer told Mada Masr that the simultaneous attack on Wad al-Mahi’s Minza and Bashkarkad and the escalation of drone strikes against Damazin pointed to a widening campaign of military pressure on the capital and its supply routes. But the attacks could also be intended to keep the military occupied and stretch its forces thin ahead of an attempt to seize its most important bases in southern Blue Nile, including Keili, Baraka, Sali and Dandaro , he added. On the Kurmuk axis, where much of the fighting over the past year has been concentrated, the RSF has deployed additional forces, a second military source said, suggesting they may launch renewed attacks on military positions in Baraka and Keili in the coming days. *** RSF fortifies West Kordofan’s Nuhud as military readies final push in North Kordofan After clearing the last major RSF defensive positions in western North Kordofan last week, the military is preparing to attack the remaining RSF-held areas in the state and advance into West Kordofan, a field source told Mada Masr. The next offensive is expected to target Um Bader and Hamra al-Sheikh in northwestern North Kordofan, with preparations already complete, the source said. Military forces have been repositioned along several fronts, with units expected to advance from Sodary and Mazroub, near the West Kordofan border, both of which the military took control of last week. North Kordofan Governor Abdel Khaleq Abdel Latif said in a press release that the military now controls 96 percent of the state. The military’s gains have come largely through a strategy of sustained pressure rather than direct assaults, a retired officer told Mada Masr. By surrounding RSF positions, cutting off supply lines and wearing down fighters with airstrikes, the military has weakened the group’s ability to hold territory and forced it to withdraw, he explained. With Mazroub now under its control, the military has greater room to maneuver, the retired officer said. It can use the area as a base to strike RSF positions in Um Bader, advance southeast toward Khawi in West Kordofan, or push southwest toward Nuhud. As the military prepares for what is intended to be the final offensive to secure North Kordofan, Mohamed Didan, the spokesperson for the special operations forces in West Kordofan, said the air force had carried out more than 150 airstrikes between Sunday and Tuesday, destroying 100 military vehicles and dozens of other targets. Anticipating a military advance into West Kordofan, the RSF has been reinforcing its positions in Nuhud. Additional forces have arrived in the city, and the group has dug trenches and built earth berms around it to guard against surprise attacks, an activist in the state told Mada Masr. Nuhud is considered the western gateway to North Kordofan’s capital, Obeid, and the northwestern corner in West Kordofan’s strategic triangle, alongside Babanusa and Heglig. Whoever holds it controls a staging point between West Kordofan and North Darfur. The Dar Hamar emergency room said on Wednesday that the RSF was also conducting forced recruitment campaigns in the city. In its statement, the emergency room said the RSF cut Starlink satellite communications in Nuhud and surrounding areas for the third consecutive day, as security restrictions on residents intensified. The group was also cutting tree branches to cover its vehicles and conceal them from aerial surveillance, the statement added. The RSF has also turned Nuhud’s main referral hospital into a base for jamming equipment and taken over West Kordofan University to house foreign fighters, according to the emergency room. These measures come as humanitarian and security conditions in Nuhud continue to deteriorate, with communications disrupted and residents facing restrictions on their movement, the emergency room said. *** Control shifts again along West Darfur border areas Border areas in West Darfur, near the Chadian border and the state capital Geneina, continue to change hands, with the military and its allied joint force of armed movements on one side and the RSF on the other vying for control. The joint force said its troops clashed with the RSF on Monday along the Bir Saliba and Abu Sorug fronts, retaking Bir Saliba and consolidating their presence in the area. The alliance also announced it destroyed seven RSF combat vehicles and inflicted heavy casualties during the operation. The latest fighting follows repeated shifts in control of the two areas, which lie about 30 and 36 km north of Geneina, which is held by the paramilitary group. In August , the joint force seized the area before pulling back to avoid being outflanked as the RSF deployed large numbers of troops and vehicles to retake it. Monday’s operation began with a surprise attack on RSF positions from several directions, inflicting casualties and destroying equipment before the joint force secured Bir Saliba, a field source in the joint force told Mada Masr. Abu Sorug is more difficult to hold because of its exposed terrain, the source said, predicting that the joint force might withdraw again toward Bir Saliba and Hajar Marfain. The two areas have remained a challenge for the RSF since the military launched a surprise offensive in West Darfur in July, advancing from North Darfur and bringing military and allied forces within reach of Geneina. The RSF has since launched several attacks in an effort to retake lost ground and ease pressure on the capital. The border location, rugged terrain and open routes toward Tina in North Darfur, which is held by the military, have made these areas particularly difficult to secure. *** RSF special operations commander defects Former RSF commander Mohamed Azrag al-Fanjary announces his defection in a video statement, October 8. Courtesy: AlArabiya Screen via YouTube. Mohamed Azrag al-Fanjary, the commander of an RSF special operations group, announced on Thursday that he defected with around 300 officers and soldiers and 30 combat vehicles, in the latest of a series of senior departures from the paramilitary group in recent months. The group included commanders and officers from units that had operated under Al-Nour “Gubba” Adam, the former senior RSF commander and Mahamid tribal leader who defected to the military earlier this year, according to a source close to Fanjary who is a member of Gubba’s defected forces. The decision followed contacts with military commanders and arrangements that had been underway for some time, the source told Mada Masr. In a video statement, Fanjary said he was relinquishing his military duties and responsibilities within the RSF, describing his decision as the result of “an honest review of oneself and deep reflection” on the state of Sudan due to the war. He disavowed abuses against civilians and their property and called on other RSF members to follow his lead. The defection is significant because of the nature of the unit that left with him, according to both the source close to Fanjary and a former RSF source who had worked in the group’s operations authority. The officers’ roles gave them knowledge of RSF deployments and operational arrangements, the sources said. According to the source close to him, Fanjary and his group decided to leave after reviewing the state of the RSF and the course of military operations in recent months. The source did not disclose where the group had been stationed or where it ultimately went. The departure involved an organized unit that kept its internal hierarchy, with officers still in command of their men and equipment, rather than individuals leaving the RSF separately, the source added. Several of the officers had been involved in field operations, giving them direct knowledge of how the RSF was deployed and operated. The source close to Fanjary placed the defection within a broader pattern among forces that had served under Gubba before his departure from the RSF. Several members of those forces, particularly field commanders, have begun holding separate discussions about leaving, the source said, adding that Fanjary was among them before he made his decision public. The former RSF operations source cautioned against interpreting the departures as evidence that the paramilitary group was collapsing. The RSF still has large units and retains significant military capabilities spread across several fronts, the source said. What Fanjary’s departure means for the RSF may become clearer in the coming days, particularly if other units that operated on the same fronts follow suit, the source close to him said. The fact that groups have been discussing their departure with military commanders makes it harder to view each case in isolation, the source added, while drawing a distinction between units that leave with their equipment and individual fighters who depart on their own. *** Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . items.title: Old Edubiase pupils turn to trading, farming as teachers’ strike disrupts schooling
items.description: Pupils of Old Edubiase Methodist Basic School in the Adansi North District of the Ashanti Region have abandoned their classrooms for farms, markets and football fields as the ongoing nationwide strike by pre-tertiary teachers disrupts academic activities. A visit to the community on Thursday, October 8, 2026, revealed school-going children engaged in various activities during school hours, with no teaching and learning taking place. While some pupils accompanied their parents to cocoa and food crop farms, carrying cutlasses and baskets, others were seen hawking boiled eggs, sachet water and other items along the principal streets of Old Edubiase. Several others loitered around the community or played football and other games under trees. In separate interviews, some pupils said their teachers had instructed them to stay at home until the strike was called off. “Our teachers told us to stay at home until we hear that the strike has been called off. That is why some of us are doing this,” a Primary Six pupil said. The pupils expressed disappointment over the industrial action, saying the prolonged absence from school was affecting their education. “We are not happy with the teachers’ strike because it is having a negative impact on our education. We have been at home for many days doing nothing,” another pupil said. The situation is particularly worrying for final-year pupils preparing for the Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE), some of whom said their mock examinations were approaching without adequate revision. “We are not happy with the teachers’ strike because it has affected our education. Our mock exam is drawing near, and the teachers are on strike. We don’t know what will happen to us,” a BECE candidate, Shadrack Amuzu, said. Parents worried about children’s welfare Parents in the community have also expressed frustration over the disruption, with some taking their children to farms to help with their work while others remain at home without supervision. Madam Yaa Nsia, a mother of three pupils at the school, said the situation had become unbearable. According to her, the strike had forced some parents to rely on their children for farm work, while others were left roaming around the community. “The strike has forced us to send our children to the farm. Some of the children are just roaming around without going to school because of the strike. This is not good for their future,” she said. She warned that the prolonged disruption could expose children to social vices, teenage pregnancy and child labour. The affected pupils and their parents have appealed to the government and teacher unions to resolve the impasse urgently to allow academic activities to resume. They urged the government to address teachers’ concerns about their conditions of service to facilitate their return to the classroom. “We are begging the government to listen to our teachers and resolve the issue for them to call off the strike. We want to go back to school,” the pupils appealed. Background to the strike Teachers across the country began a nationwide strike over what they describe as the government’s failure to address concerns about their conditions of service, including deprived-area allowances, promotion issues and other welfare matters. The industrial action has disrupted teaching and learning in basic schools, while some senior high schools have also recorded low attendance as parents keep their children at home. The Ghana Education Service (GES) and the Ministry of Education have held meetings with the teacher unions, including the Ghana National Association of Teachers (GNAT), the National Association of Graduate Teachers (NAGRAT) and the Coalition of Concerned Teachers (CCT), but a breakthrough has yet to be achieved. Residents of Old Edubiase are calling for urgent intervention by the Adansi North District Directorate of Education, traditional authorities and the government to ensure pupils return to the classroom before the disruption causes further damage to the academic calendar.

items.title: Cinkassé/4e session ordinaire : Les travaux portent sur le budget primitif 2027
items.description: Cinkassé, 9 oct. (ATOP) – Le conseil municipal de la commune de Cinkassé 1 a ouvert, le jeudi 8 octobre à Cinkassé, les travaux de la 4ᵉ session ordinaire de l’année 2026, consacrée notamment à l’élaboration du budget primitif, exercice 2027. Les travaux porteront également sur le débat d’orientation budgétaire, des sorties de terrain pour recueillir les besoins des communautés, des échanges avec certaines catégories socioprofessionnelles ainsi que la révision de la délibération relative aux taxes communales. Le préfet de Cinkassé, colonel Yanani Tiékabe, a souligné que le budget primitif 2027 doit s’inscrire dans la droite ligne de la feuille de route gouvernementale 2026-2031, tout en tenant compte des réalités et des priorités de la commune. Le maire de Cinkassé 1, Nagnango Koundjo, a indiqué que l’adoption d’un budget réaliste, équilibré et adapté aux besoins des populations constitue une étape essentielle pour poursuivre les actions de développement local. Il a exhorté les acteurs à s’impliquer davantage dans les activités de mobilisation des ressources financières de la commune. ATOP/BB/JK/MD

items.title: Yémen: «Sur le plan économique, la société est livrée à elle-même et sur la sécurité, c’est un totalitarisme géré par la peur»
items.description: Après des années d'accalmie, la guerre au Yémen s'est réveillée et entre dans une nouvelle phase. Les affrontements font rage sur plusieurs fronts depuis plusieurs jours, à l’intérieur des terres et sur les hauteurs surplombant les régions côtières récemment conquises par les houthistes. RFI s'est concentrée vendredi 9 octobre sur cette guerre qui sévit, provoquant l’une des pires crises humanitaires au monde et asphyxiant une population déjà épuisée par plus d'une décennie de conflit. Le décryptage de Mustafa Naji Aljabzi, sociologue et chercheur indépendant yéménite.

items.title: La CAN pourrait rester tous les deux ans : la CAF fait marche arrière
items.description: Un an après avoir tourné la page, la CAF pourrait la rouvrir. Selon The Guardian, l'instance s'apprête à renoncer à une CAN tous les quatre ans et à revenir au rythme biennal qui a fait la tradition du tournoi depuis 1957. Patrice Motsepe a lui-même confirmé, vendredi, au Cap-Vert, que la question était à l'étude. Il s'exprimait lors de la conférence de presse de clôture de la conférence stratégique de la CAF. Un vote est attendu au comité exécutif. Aucune décision définitive n'a été officialisée. Le revirement serait spectaculaire. Le 20 décembre 2025, à Rabat, la veille du coup d'envoi de la CAN marocaine, le comité exécutif avait acté le passage à un cycle de quatre ans. Les éditions 2027 (Kenya, Tanzanie, Ouganda) et 2028 étaient maintenues, puis le tournoi devait devenir quadriennal. Une Ligue des nations africaine annuelle, lancée en 2029, devait combler le vide. La CAF avait même ouvert les candidatures pour 2028, 2032 et 2036. Dès l'origine, la méthode avait fait grincer des dents. The Guardian avait rapporté que l'instance était accusée d'avoir imposé la réforme sans consulter pleinement ses fédérations membres. Le projet de Gianni Infantino, qui plaidait depuis des années pour un calendrier quadriennal, avait pourtant été longtemps repoussé par la CAF. La raison était simple : la CAN pèse environ 80 % de ses revenus. L'argument de Motsepe était alors la compensation annuelle de la future Ligue des nations. Il n'a visiblement pas convaincu. Les critiques sont venues des supporters, des fédérations, des observateurs. Elles portaient sur la visibilité des sélections nationales, l'attrait commercial du tournoi et sa place dans le calendrier international. Pour beaucoup de pays, une CAN tous les deux ans est la seule vitrine continentale régulière. Ce serait aussi un nouveau revers pour le président de la CAF. Son projet d'élargir la CAN de 24 à 28 équipes, présenté en février, avait déjà été rejeté par le comité exécutif. Deux membres anonymes avaient alors dénoncé un manque de concertation. Un retour au rythme biennal serait lu comme un désaveu pour Motsepe. Et pour Infantino, dont la FIFA voulait faire de l'Afrique un laboratoire du calendrier quadriennal, comme un camouflet. Reste à savoir si le vote confirmera la bascule. Le football africain, lui, a déjà tranché. Cheikh Gora DIOP
